Review:
My 2.5 yr old has so much fun with the balance bike, that he inherited from his 4 yr old brother, they ride bikes together almost daily. We had to remove the cap/ plug on the bottom of the bike to allow the pipe for the seat to go lower than designed - it wasn't difficult to do, it allowed my just 24 month old son to start riding. It took a few weeks to get used to sitting rather than walking with the bike. Now he is 2.5 and he has done a couple miles bike tours with the family. My older son went from the balance bike to a 12" kid's bike within 10 min of teaching himself, he was 3.5 yrs old, he never had training wheels. He transitioned to 14" a few weeks later. The little guy will be ready for a real bike by 3 yrs age the latest, probably earlier. I wish the video posting worked on Amazon but it doesn't, it is incredible how much speed the balance bike allows, and how small of a curve the kids can ride with it. We take this balance bike everywhere, it's light, rides well on all kind of surfaces, and beats the slow walk of a toddler any day. Downside, toddlers don't have the coordination to hand break and balance the bike at the same time, and toddler hands are not strong enough to pull the hand break, therefore shoes take a beating. 3 yr olds can pull the break though. Other downside, it's not for 4 yr or older kids, the highest seat setting will not allow the legs to stretch out enough, we tried it with a friend's kid. Well, the idea is that the kid can ride a real bike by age 4.
Compared to other balance bikes: way better than wooden bikes, way more durable than many other metal bikes (ours went through 2 yrs of all weather conditions, it gets mostly left outside - summer, winter...), best of all are the rubber air tires, and it has hand breaks.

Reason for 4 stars, I read that the bike is no longer made with air inflatable rubber tires, one of it's best features. I hope they go back to that.

This review is for the Schwinn Huron 26 inch cruiser bike (one-speed and coaster brakes).

Great bike. Easily put together. Just a couple of minor problems that cost this review one star.

First, the kick stand is about 1/4 inch too long. With the kick stand down and engaged, the bike stands almost perfectly straight up instead of at a very slight lean. This makes it real easy to topple it. In fact, I stopped along the road to remove some debris from the road. A car passing by caused a burst of air and toppled my bike. The bike now has a few scratches that it should not have.

Second, within a few days I was having to air up the tires. At first, it was every other day and then became every day. I took the tires off and replaced the tubes. I put the old tubes in the bathtub with enough air in them to inflate them some. There were no outright holes, but you could see air bubbles all over the surface of the tubes. The rubber was just that weak.

Even with these two flaws, I love this bike.

Review:
Love, love, love this bike. Our toddler young'un received this as a gift from his very generous grandparents, and this has quickly put all his other toys to shame. He now tools around the driveway over and over and over, while we try to catch up with him so that he doesn't fall.

1) Does the young'un fall all the time?

Yes and no. At first, yes, all the time, because he didn't know how to maintain his balance. Now, he doesn't fall as much because his balance is better, but he also keeps his feet on the ground more because he is more scared of falling. So, I think he's getting better and learning his balance more, and that's the cool part of this bike--he's really getting his confidence up. In fact, when he was riding a friend's tricycle at the park the other day, he somehow knew exactly what to do even though the tricycle is obviously different with its pedals and third wheel.

Given that falls do happen, we use close supervision and a helmet, and all the running to catch up with him is quite the workout.

2) Is the bike sturdy?

It's very sturdy--that might be the most impressive part of this little bike. I can't believe how well made it is for a tiny balance bike. (In fact, I hadn't even heard of balance bikes until we received this.) The wheels are rubber and are thick, which is great for durability and also balance. I believe this will last for as long as our young'un can use it.

3) Will the kid want to/be able to use it for a while?

This is a trickier question, but I think so. Our young'un is tall, but he's all legs, so this fits him for now at approx. 2 1/2 years old. But, we have the seat very low. I do not believe a small 2 1/2 year old would be able to use this, but that's just my own impression.

As for how long he can use this, the seat goes up quite a bit, so we're hoping that he can use this at least for a couple more years. By then, we think he'll be balancing well enough for a real bike... maybe?

If we hadn't received this as a gift and if I had known what a balance bike was, we absolutely would have bought this for our young'un. It's a really nifty idea, and Schwinn has executed it extraordinary well. Highly recommended!

Review:
I bought this bike as a travel bike. It surpasses that in every way and is a regular bike I ride, not just when traveling. My main bike is a Surly Disk Trucker. I have built it for long distance riding/touring. It is a great bike, also, however I can't take it with me on a lot of my trips. That is where the Dahon Mariner D8 comes in. With the gear range (30"-90"), fenders, and the rear rack standard on the bike it is an amazingly rideable bike as a stock bike. I was impressed with it from the first time I rode it.

The only "change" from the stock bike/components I have made thus far is I swapped the pedals for combo platform/SPD clipless. Due to some knee problems in past years from riding all my mileage riding is with SPD pedals/shoes. However, the ability to switch to platforms helps me when I need to make a quick jaunt in regular shoes or if I am high on miles and I need to give my calf muscles a break by shifting my foot positions (that I can't do while clipped in).

The gear range on the bike (30"-90") has been OK for most riding I have done. However, I do wish it had more low-end gearing for climbing hills. On the top end I find the gearing adequate as I won't be going faster than I could pedal in top gear on this bike anyway.

I did rate this 4 stars for "sturdiness". For what the bike is, it is a very stable bike and I have no problem riding it. I ride it regularly. However, one must understand from the get-go that the smaller wheel bikes are "twitchy" compared to regular wheel size bikes (26", 700c, etc). That isn't a bad thing, just expect it and if you do I'm sure you will also find the bike very ridable as I do.

For comfort I rated the bike as 4 stars. The reason for this is I don't find the straight bars "comfortable". That is just me. I get nerve and circulation problems in my hands so I constantly move my hand positions to circumvent that (on every bike). My hand positions are quite limited on the straight bar. That is one of my future upgrades - bars that give me more positions (probably drops, but not sure just yet). I will say, though, for me the stock saddle is very comfortable. Depending on the length of my ride I may not even put on bike shorts. If I'm riding all day the combination of the saddle and bike shorts is great.

As for set up out-of-the-box - if you are a decent bike mechanic you can set it up. The wheels need aligned, brakes need adjusted, magnet clip (folded bike has the frame halves that lock together with a magnet clip) needs aligned, the rear derailleur needs adjusted, and the chain guard on the down tube needs adjusted. One note on the chain guard - adjust this so it is close to the top of the chain and it isn't rubbing the side of the chain. I have had the chain bounce up and through the gap in the guard on a ride where it was a challenge getting the chain down on the ring. Once adjusted it shouldn't give you any trouble. Fold latches should be "tight", but you shouldn't have to muscle them closed. There are adjustment nuts to tune the pressure. You want the latches under good pressure, not loose, and not super tight. I have never had any sense of the joints being "loose" or feeling like the frame was going to open or bars fold while I've been on it - very sturdy design. The rear derailleur may take a few tweaks to operate without a hitch. I didn't get everything dialed in on my bike until about 50 miles. Its all smooth now.

Don't throw anything away from the box/packaging until you have the documents and parts. There is a small bottle of paint they give you also. It should be in the small parts box with the pedals etc.

For my phone holder on the bike I use a RAM QuickGrip on the lower steer tube with an X-Grip mount. I use a piece of string or a zip tie to lock the phone in place so it doesn't bounce out. There are other phone mounts RAM makes, I just haven't tried them. The combination I use works and I have another X-Grip I use with a 7" tablet as well. I use the tablet for larger scale mapping/navigating/trip recording on some long rides. My main bike computer is a Garmin Edge 1000, however (in the pics of the bike set up that is what goes on the bar accessory mount, then my phone is just used as a phone and to compare routing to Google Maps when needed).

If you are looking for a do-everything compact bike to take with you, or you deal with small spaces for storage on a regular basis (between home and commuting to work, for example) - this is a fantastic bike so long as you expect the "twitchyness" from the small wheels and don't expect to be climbing many hills.

Two upgrades on the horizon for my uses of the Mariner D8 are:
- Handlebars - more ergonomic/more hand positions
- 2 chain rings and front derailleur - I may bump the large 53t ring there now up a hair just to have an extra higher gear combo and add a smaller one around 40-47t so I can drop down low in the hills

Last note on panniers on the stock rack -
I use the "front" panniers of my Ortleib Packer Plus series, the Sport Packer Plus's, as rear panniers at times. I have the clip mounts to where the bags are as far back on the rack as I can get them. I have no problems with heel strike at all. A lot of people and bike shops probably will advise against loading a folding bike down due to clearance issues, but I have not found that to be the case at all. I wear size 10 shoes and use SPD clips. The combination with the bike and panniers is a winner for me. If you tried to get larger rear panniers on the bike you would be in for some issues on two fronts - drag on the ground when leaning in turns in addition to heel strike - unless you could come up with a way to extend the bags to the rear further. This, however, may change the handling of the bike with the weight distribution.

Would I buy the bike again? Absolutely!
Would I recommend the bike to others? Absolutely! And I let them go for a test ride on it too if we get the chance.

Review:
We received both of our bikes yesterday after about a week of shipping time, which is reasonable considering it does contain batteries. Both were very well packed and protected and in VERY large boxes!

The unpacking was very easy, although the assembly was a bit more challenging. There were a few times where the instructions weren't terrible specific and we had to puzzle things together, but in the end it all made sense. It took about an hour to put together the first back and no more than a half hour for the second one.

I would definitely recommend keeping some pictures of the finished product on-hand so you can refer to it just to make sure everything is facing in the right direction.

Once they were assembled and inflated, they worked like a charm! The electric motor has a decent kick to it without being overpowered, the pedal action and gear shifting is nice and smooth, and the control module was very easy to manage without being confusing at all.

Folding it was extremely easy as well. Just lift up a lever, pull out, and it folds in half easily. You can carry an allen wrench with you to rotate the handlebars as well if you need additional room, but we were able to fold and store both bikes under our staircase with little to no trouble at all, taking up far less space than the two fully assembled bikes would.

There is a decent amount of weight to the bikes, probably about 45-50 pounds without the batteries. We're having a hitch installed on our car so that we can carry them around due to the weight, but they certainly aren't unmanageable by any means (and I'm hardly in great shape - hence getting the bikes in the first place!).

If you're looking to experience a Class 2 electric bike I would definitely recommend this one. The price was right, the weight limit is very welcoming to those of us who are stockier/heavier, and the riding experience is an absolute joy. Assembly was a bit confusing the first time around but once it's together it's very easy to figure out and use, and can be a great gateway bike to serious bicycling!

As a side note: Look into whether your area has any Rides-To-Trails. I highly recommend them!

I just needed to adjust the front disc brake and lube the chain.  After 75 miles biking, I decided to make minor adjustments to the front and rear derailleur. New bikes will get cable stretch and need adjustment after break-in.  The front derailleur was making a ticking  noise which was the chain rubbing.  I looked at a couple of videos on adjusting the front and rear derailleurs. I made adjustment and the bike shifts smoother and quieter.  The disc brakes are good, but my 20 year old Specialized mountain bike with "V" brakes are better.  The tires are 700 X 38c which equate to 28" X 1.5" and are perfect size for a hybrid bike.  The seat was comfortable, I do not understand all the critics about the seat.  My Specialized mountain bike seat is much harder. The GTX seat is not as comfortable as a fat, dual spring cruiser seat, but those seats can cause chaffing.  The bike rides smooth, fast and comfortable with the help of the front suspension forks.  Also, the bike looks good.  The 18" frame is perfect for me at 5' 11" and 210 lbs.  Some have criticized the chain braking and tires pinching.  I keep the chain lubed, shift gears property by avoiding chain stress gear shifting and have no issues.  I keep 65 psi (max 70 psi)  in the tires and have no issues of pinched tires. I find 65 psi a good balance for both speed and comfort. The Schwinn Elite GTX is exactly what I wanted .  A Hybrid bike that is quicker and more comfortable on the road or gravel than my Specialized mountain bike.  i would recommend the Schwinn  Elite GTX hybrid bike.  Pricing will vary depending on supply and demand, but i paid $450 shipped and can't complain.  Most aluminum frame bikes with shimano derailleurs, disc brakes and front suspension cost around $600 plus.  This bike is a good value when supply can fulfill demand at $450.

Review:
Full disclosure, I have never owned an electric bike before, have not had to deal with customer service and am pretty easy to please. All that being said, this bike is AWESOME! For starters it came much quicker than expected. The instructions are decent, could be better though. It took a while to figure out that there is a protective disc to be removed and discarded from each side of the motor near the wheel. I also put a couple of parts on backwards and then was like 'huh, well that doesnt seem right". After staring at the instructions for a few minutes (per section) I got it. Again, full disclosure, I was super high when I put my bike together. That being said, I was able to put this bike together with pretty much no problems despite being high, it shouldn't be a problem for you.

Now for the meat and potatoes of the review, performance. I have been riding and playing around for a couple of days now and I am very impresesed. I wouldn't say that I "stress tested" the bike, but have put it through various normal conditions such as sidewalks, grass, dirt roads, gravel and.... well, some puddles. Nothing crazy, but all things faced buy average commuters. I found no immediate sign of air loss in the tires, no bending or shifting of the alignment and no loose electrical componants.

The interface is easy to understand and you can easily feel the motor kick on once the bike chain has been engaged for about one second. I actually looked at the controls and thought "easy peasy, no need to read how to use them" and spent the first day using only peddle assist mode. I figured the setting below "low" was basically "still on but no power to the motor", for just the light and horn or something. I was mistaken. I realized just as I got home from my first day of trying out my new bike that there is an *actual*, twisting throttle EXPERTLY blended into the inner part of the handle bar. I just so happen to grip my handles super close to the edge AND DIDN'T EVEN NOTICE THE THROTTLE. I had a good laugh about that. The mode beneath "low" would be "throttle only". Womp womp.

So yeah, super great bike. Goes pretty fast, handles well, looks nice, read the instructions.

Edit 1: I do have one tiny complaint. Merely aesthetic but it says "ELECTRIC VEHICLE" in small but bold text on each side. I actually taped over that with black electrical tape. Every time I went to lock up the bike I saw the words thought to myself "Well, glad they know which bike to steal." I have had a $40 bike lock cut with bolt cutters for a $100 Walmart bike. Again, a very small complaint but the advertisement seems like extra incentive to would be thieves and it terrifies me 😱

Review:
I was looking for a bike to ride with my 4 yr old son for the summer.
In the past, I've had to take my cheap bike rack and strap it on my itty bitty toyota.
This takes much time, and is a bit cumbersome, especially when trying to install a child seat, etc.
So I thought, hmmm.... folding bike? That sure would be more convenient.
Throw them both in the trunk, and I'm ready to go.

So off I went researching potential products. Here's what I found out:

Now, I've been researching bikes for three weeks in order to purchase something.
My budget isn't very extensive really - about 400 max.

I wanted something that was durable and simple . . . and most importantly - safe.

Here's what I discovered . . . from many of the reviews I read - some things to note-
- There are some folding bike reviews that describe stories of hinges that break or loosen where the bike folds
- Folding pedals might be a plus for storage, but on some models these pedals seem to fail routinely if anchored into a cheap crankset
- According to reviews, most entry level folding bikes don't seem to really be intended for the day to day abuse of commuting
- Most reviews proclaimed that light recreational use on most entry level models was great, but once bikes were used more regularly for
traveling or commutes, parts began to fail - so good components really matter.
- All of the above comments seemed to appear more than once for various models - so read the reviews - or the good ones anyway.

I wanted a bike that could be easily serviced over its lifespan:
I looked heavily into some Dahon Models, such as the Vybe C7A, Speed D7 and even (especially) Speed Uno.
All are really good bikes, but . . .
According to many reviews, Dahon doesn't seem to offer good customer service in the US, unless you live near a dealer, which I do not.
So if a component on the bike breaks, where and how do I get a new one? I'm sure this is possible, but not easy.
The Speed Uno is nice looking - but coaster breaks are not efficient at stopping the bike. The pedals on this model seemed to have issues too.
I looked heavily into Retrospec. Very reasonably priced and good looking stuff. But good luck on trying to get anyone to email you back.
Again, what do I do if something arrives broken or breaks on the bike? Sure, it's possible, but not easy.

But you know what's easy? You can look up Allen Sports, and they've got a phone number - not just a twitter account - but like a REAL phone number! In fact there's even THREE on their website AND and email address. You can call and talk to a REAL PERSON and get help - and parts!!
Wow man! Sign me up!

I don't need a bike small enough to fit into a suitcase - and this guy is a little on the big side when folded - so what.
You can fold the thing up - the wheels lock together with a METAL COMPONENT that is WELDED to the FRAME! So Cool!
That's really good folks - and not common apparently. After that, the bike and be strolled around like a funny looking
little grocery cart, so it's still quite portable when you're on your feet in spite of its weight.

Finally, the folding mechanism on this thing is apparently pretty solid - and the frame is too - just read the "foldingbike20" website reviews.
I highly recommend this site by the way. The frame and that folding mechanism really matter oodles - esp. if you plan to use the bike more regularly. Other models didn't seem to measure up to this test with regular use. Stuff seems to break down. Pins fall out, stuff comes unscrewed - things get loose - right at the heart of the bike. This one apparently though is pretty stout.

So why am I only giving this thing only four stars? Because I will receive it tomorrow finally! Woohoo!
So I will confirm my theories shortly with more info. to follow.
All of you out there who are about to purchase a folding bike - you cannot go wrong with a price point on this thing for 300+ bucks.
With what I've found out so far, I feel confident I've made the right choice.

Review:
The bike is a great value. Made of 6061 Aluminum, it is both stronger and lighter than bikes made 10 or 15 years ago. The shifting group on the bike is entry level but more than sufficient for this level of bike. The brakes are wonderful, and the tires, although heavy, are quite acceptable. The front shock is pretty much crap but shouldn't cause you trouble (i.e. it is unlikely to break), only extra effort. Overall, though, it is hard to find as much bike as this at this price level. The big brand names cannot touch this bike at this price.

So, should you buy it?

To answer this question, you have to ask yourself, "What do I want out of riding?" There are many valid answers to this question, so think about it. Are you planning on riding the local gravel trail in town? Are you planning on short trips around with the kids? Would you prefer to ride actually two-track trails with roots, stumps, rocks and sand? Or are you looking to do distance riding with friends?

Answering these questions honestly will go a long way toward deciding whether this bike is for you. So what is this bike best used for? This bike is almost exclusively for riding gravel trails around town with the occasional off-road or two track. It is NOT meant for riding around town and definitely not for distance riding. Similarly, it shouldn't be bought if you plan on riding technical trails with drops and steep climbs.

Let me back up my unfounded statements. Gravel trails are easy to ride and you could easily get away with a touring bike (defined as thinner tires and a more upright, laid back riding style). But every so often, you will hit a patch that could puncture your tire and/or tube on a touring bike. The Kenda tires and soft shock will keep that from happening on the Response. Similarly, the low gear ratios on this bike will make riding up hills much easier, as long as the path is not too rough. If you are doing steep inclines on a bumpy road, the crap shock that comes with this bike will feel like a pogo-stick, causing the front tire to lose grip with the road/trail. This will most likely end with you walking the bike up. But in well maintained trails, you should excel.

If you are riding around town, you'll see lots of surburbanites riding their Treks and Specialized mountain bikes. You would fit right in with this bike. However, you would be better served by a touring (sometimes called "hybrid") bike. Something like this: [[ASIN:B002LFRT24 Diamondback Edgewood Men's Comfort Hybrid Bike (700c Wheels)]]

I know, it is not as cool looking. And looks should factor in since you want to feel good when riding around town. But that less cool looking will translate into higher speeds, less effort, and more comfort. If, on the other hand, you are planning on riding technical trails, you will need more gear. You could buy a better front fork (at a minimum, something like this: [[ASIN:B000NNSY2U RockShox Tora Coil 302 U-Turn Fork (Black Pl Rim/Disc, 85-130)]] ) but really, you'd be better off spending more on a lighter, more complete bike. You should expect to spend at least 50% more on an entry level bike for more serious downhill and technical trails. If you are over 5'10", you might even consider a 29-inch mountain bike.

Finally, if you want to do distance riding, the bike is wholly inappropriate. The riding stance and the tire thickness would make this bike (or any mountain bike) a poor choice for anyone other than the most fit athlete out there.

In summary, this is a GREAT value bike, oodles better than anything you find at your local discount market. Moreover, Giant, Specialized, and Trek cannot touch this price point and, although you must compromise on weight, front fork, and grouping, you will get a whole lot of bike for a low price.

By the way, yes, I both own and ride this bike, along with my Giant TCX Crossbike.

UPDATE: The day I wrote my review, the bike was on sale. Now that the price is back up, I would knock off a 1/2 a star, since the value is diminished. I'm not saying it's not worth Amazon's price, only that if I were you, I would consider waiting for a sale.

Review:
First surprise out of the box was the badging: Kingttu instead of Eurobike. But I noticed it was identical to the Eurobike--including Eurobike badging elsewhere on the frame, etc. Different name, same bike. Second surprise was no quick release on front wheel as mentioned in the manual. But I couldn't see that on photos of the bike itself online. Third surprise was the rims seemed to wobble. I first thought they must be bent or not trued correctly. But long story short it turned out that the tires were molded improperly. Fortunately the manufacturer was very good and responsive about correcting that situation and I was able to get the tires replaced. They were polite, apologetic and cooperative.

Also fortunate that the next surprise was a good one: The bike didn't need much of anything as far as adjustment. Just a little tightening up here and there. First time in decades of biking that I didn't have to adjust anything out of the box so to speak.

And now having ridden it for a bit, I will need to adjust the front derailleur. And not very much. This is perfectly normal. On Any bike the cables stretch, and so one or more of the derailers usually need a bit of adjustment after a few rides. Bikes are not plug and play... Please do not be upset if they need some adjustment right off the bat or shortly thereafter.

Speaking of riding, especially at this price point the bike handles well. As I'm a little older now I'm not exactly a boulder hopping maniac anymore. But I did hit some appreciable speeds on decent trails. No complaints.

Speaking of which... I strongly believe value/performance for the money is the most important measure. This bike is not perfect. But neither is my old Pontiac, which is economical, reliable, practical... But it would be ludicrous to compare it to a Porsche, a BMW... But sadly in all manner of reviews I see such "apples and peaches" comparisons all the time. But again for the money, I'm very happy with the bike. In going to the bike shop (something I try to avoid at nearly all costs because I'm invariably told directly or indirectly how crappy my cheap bike truly is) I told them about a $150 mountain bike that I rode hard for nearly 20 years. And it was still fine. I just needed to upgrade to one with a suspension. (I won't mention the brand as they have gone downhill in quality.) In the meantime I had acquired a few other cheap bikes which at best were not very good. This Kingttu/Eurobike is much better. The only remaining question is how long it will hold up over time. But I don't foresee unreasonable problems.

And again as a matter of proper perspective, most of what are considered to be true trail bikes for the serious enthusiast cost thousands of dollars. (The cheapest bike in the shop where I went was around $1, 300. And that's with no suspension.) But for the average user, for someone like myself looking for easy to moderate trails or for some street riding, this bike fits the bill. But for someone looking to do heavy use on more brutal trails, at this price point you are comparing a Porsche to a Pontiac. My car wouldn't last at high speed or perform anywhere near as well as the Porche, but that doesn't mean it's not a good car (At over 230,000 miles it still gets over 30 miles per gallon and barely uses any oil.) And directly that this isn't a good bike. Suspension bikes ironically are more delicate because they have more moving parts. That older bike I had forever had no suspension. I have little doubt if it did it would not have lasted nearly as long. As they wear out suspension bikes start to handle wonky and can become unsafe without proper maintenance--which can become cost prohibitive on an old bike.

So... Yes, for the money this is a very good bike. Comfortable ride. Handles well. Nice gear range. I like the shifters... No complaints. (But as always as I'm north of 50 I replaced the seat for more comfort. And the pedals as well as that's something I've done on every bike I've ever gotten. I like a little bit more grip so I don't slip off. And they nearly always seem the cheapest or worst part of a bike straight out of the box. I've also tossed in some more bucks for other modifications like bullhorn grips on the handlebars, and a carrier and pack so I can repair the bike if necessary on the trail. But again I would do the same for any bike. It truly isn't fun to break down or get a flat miles from nowhere with no means to repair the bike--and that has happened to me. Lesson learned.

And before I end this review I should talk a little bit about brakes. One of the main reasons I chose this bike is I've noticed that most others in my price range essentially now have side pull brakes. As delicately and politely as I can put it, they are not fun to work on. They are not reliable... Center pull are fine but I was surprised that I didn't see them anywhere. Unlike the side pull, they pull equally on each brake pad and so a whole bucket full of problems are averted.

As for disc brakes, they work great but I would recommend watching a video or two about how to properly break them in and care for them. Mine started to squeal and I learned a few things as I had never had them before. They are now fine. (I just cleaned them up a bit in this case. Didn't need to pull the pads or anything.) But in general they should be properly broken in and maintained. Again bikes are not plug and play...

(As a PostScript since writing this review I've done some research as I couldn't seem to find center pull brakes anywhere. Sadly they've become mostly obsolete... pretty much relegated to "vintage" bikes. (Apparently I'm showing my age.) I read that side pull brakes are "better" as they are easier to adjust. I sincerely hope they have Vastly improved over the years because that was definitively Never my experience with them. Center pull brakes provide more road clearance as well, and the Only time I needed to touch them was when changing out brake pads. That's it. Can't say the same for side pull brakes (I even went to a bike shop or two to have my side pull brakes adjusted and they didn't have any better success than I did. A waste of time and money.) But they are cheaper to manufacture so I think that plays into the equation quite heavily. So personally I'm going to play it safe and stick with disc brakes.)

Review:
The concept of a collapsible, dual suspension electric bike with disc brakes sounds amazing. The reality is far less impressive. I spent years as a bicycle cop, riding Treks that were capable and durable. This bike does not offer that confidence. It has the fit and finish of Chinese metal. You will always wish you had something just a little better.

When I first put it together I charged up the bike and took it out with naive excitement to have the wind whip through what remains of my flowing locks. The bike would not run on any level above 1 without automatically shutting off. The seller was responsive and sent me a second battery. Unfortunately, I continued to have the same issue.

I researched these Chinese bikes a little more in attempting to fix the problem. It appears these battery packs often have recycled or reused battery cells that may have faults. In order to get them to work they need to be charged well beyond just getting it to full charge the first time. That fixed one battery, but not the original that came with the bike.

I did eventually get the bike to work even though the battery won't lock into the cradle that holds it. It just rests there. Now that it is working, it is exhilarating to ride. It has nice power and pull to it. However, I'm 5'9" and the frame is just a hair too small for me. It has since become my daughter's bike and she loves it. It now makes it very difficult to keep up with a 10 year old on my old 21 speed. But she sure is happy, and far less tired than the old man.

I highly suggest getting an electric bike. It brings the joy back to riding. This is likely not the one you want. If yours does not work, it is quite expensive to send it back. I would look for one with more and better reviews.

Review:
Update #3, 2017-09-23. Adding photos and some more riding and maintenance notes. You can also see some videos I am posting on YouTube for this bike.

I had a spare mechanical disk brake caliper available, with slightly bigger brake pads and disk, so I installed it in place of the original front brake setup. I did it because my original front brake was not operating smoothly (with a pulsing feel, which could lead to an easier wheel lock-up on sand or slippery surfaces). The new brake is smooth. The original rear brake is smooth too. I suspect the original front disk was not of uniform thickness, causing the pulsation (it was true and straight).

I did a couple of range tests and it seems the asvertised range is realistic. Ebikes' range is highly dependent on how one rides them, the terrain, weight of the rider, tire pressure, etc. I did my 25 mile round-trip commute to work almost exclusively in PAS 4 (assist level 4 out of 5), with some lower assist levels here and there when I needed to slow down and almost no level 5 assist (max). Starting at 42V fully charged battery, I came back hone at 36.7V, which is not bad - I could probably pedal at keast another 10 miles the same way, for a total of well over 30 miles. That was done at speeds faster than most regular bikes with recreational riders on them, with less effort, but a little sllower than full on race or light commuter bikes with strong and determined riders on them. The trip has many long not steep hills, some shirt steep ones, and almost no flat areas. Average spees was about 12 miles ler hour. On another trip, I went faster and managed to empty the battery complety in only about 20 miles, using a good mix of PAS 4 and 5. If I stay on PAS 5 all the time, I suspect I won't get more than 15 miles at full power in the typical hilly terrain around here. On flat roads, with 20psi or more in the tires, I think it will do better, but hub motors don't like hills and become inefficient (compared to mid-drives) at slow speeds and steep hills.

Bottom line, if looking for a fun bike that can keep-up (and then some) with regular recreational riders on regular bikes, and you don't have many long steep hills, this is a good option. If you expect it to perform like a more powerful and efficient mid-drive bike, you will be disappointed.

The motor is not loud but is not silent. It is quieter than the tires in most situations, except at full load during acceleration before it reaches cruising speed at whatever PAS level. There is some gear noise that is not terrible but compared to my Bafang BBSHD drive, which is virtually silent, this is a bit noisier under load.

The 5 PAS levels are not spaced very well and I think the power ramps-up a bit too aggressively from stop or low speeds. Say the bike is in PAS 3, which tops out at a very reasonable 15 miles per hour or so. From a stop or slower speeds the bike tries to apply full power, and only gradually reduces power very close to top speed for the PAS level. I would prefer lower power in the first three lower PAS modes but higher speed limits. PAS 4 and 5 can be more powerful, this is OK. But I want a mode that would keep-up 10-15 miles without overzealously trying to accelerate to that speed every time I slow down a bit. Having throttle would be helpful for that, but the controller does not provide connections for one (alternative controllers can be had for $15-$30 that supprt a throttle, and I might upgrade mine down the road).

Update #2, 2017-09-17. I finished adjusting the bike. I further fine-tuned brakes, so now they are firm and strong. I can lock the rear wheel easily and the front is plenty strong too. They are very noisy (screechy), feel rough, and the stopping is not smoothly uniform as the disk turns through each full rotation. Will give them a few more miles and hard stops to see if they settle any better against the disks. Maybe they need further adjustment and cleaning... A few other things are now apparent. First, the deraileur is bent out of shape, and I think whoever assembled the bike did it on purpose - if it is straight, it rubs against the rim in 1st gear and the chain rubs against the tire. The motor vibrates a bit around 20-24kmh under power (PAS 4 and 5). The vibration is felt through the frame and seat and is heard as the rear disk resonates and vibrates and makes a buzzing sound noise. This is only in max power mode, level 5 assist. The bike is smooth and more quiet at lpwer and faster speeds, and no issues under pedal power only at any speed. This only develops under hard acceleration. I'll call the seller and Vilano bikes tomorrow to see if they can help resolve the situation, as this noise is not normal. It seems to imlrove as the bike breaks in (or maybe I am getting used to it).

2017-09-17, day one, morning riding. Surprisingly good power on uphills - I am 200 lb and it can't climb the steepest hills without pedaling help, but makes it very easy, and no issues with medim-steep hills. The spokes are not tensioned enough, especially on the rear wheel - they vibrate audibly at full power, will need to tension them more. This bike stands quite high above the ground: the frame seems like it is made for and can accomodate 24" wheels with up to 2" tires - lots of clearance on the 20" fat tires (except on the side of the rear tire with the chain. The tall tires and large frame bring the pedals quite high above the ground. Good clearance, but at proper saddle height, I can't reach the ground with my foot. That would not be an issue if you like to ride with the seat low, but if you like to ride with the seat up and set for road riding with good leg extension, you may need to be coming off the bike at stops. The battery seems OK so far. I only did about 8 miles this morning at moderate speeds and some hills, and the charge is still well above 36V. So at medium assist levels I expect to be able to do at least 20-30 miles per charge. Range test will need to wait until the wheels are tensioned. One problem is that the display does not show voltage, only a graphic of the battery state of charge. I can see there is sag under full power, but do not know how many volts. I am measuring the battery voltage with multimeter at the bike light wires or the battery terminals when the bike is stopped. The fat tires absorb imperfections in the road very well. The frame is quite sturdy for a folder, though some flex is felt in the steerer. The bike is stable at speed, does not wobble and can ride hands off, but like any small-wheeled bike it is not as stable as a big-wheeled one. More to follow ...

First impressions below (2017-09-16 ):

I just received the Vilano Neutron bike, assembled it, and rode around the block for a few minutes. So this is just an initial impressions light review. Will update as I ride the bike more. I will add video soon.

Super fast shipping from Florida. Came well-packed with no damage at all due to shipping. Good fit and finish, better than I expected from a $550 ebike.

Assembly is easy if you have done basic bike assembly. No tools are included. You will need hex wrenches, philips head screwdriver, and flat and/or socket wrenches for assembly and adjustmet.

Adjustment is not optional! The bike will not work eell or at all without it! Plan to pay for it if you can't do it yourself, but it is basic and standard, so any bike shop could do it. Amazon offers free assembly, take it if you are not sure you can do it (but learn to do it, it is fairly easy, you will need to do it again in the future).

The bike comes with a big, but generic english manual, so many instructions are not relevant to this particular bike. And key instructions are missing. Thre are *no* online instructions on the manufacturer web site for this model either. What is missing is important - how to operate and setup the computer and how to connect the light (the two wires for the front light are unmarked as are the connectors on the back of the light, so unclear which is positive and which is negative - this is a 36V LED light, and unclear if it matters or not if one were to swap the cables).

My bike came almost fully charged, reading 41V (fully chsrged is about 42V, the battery rating is 36V nominal, 8.8Ah. No info on the cell chemistry or individual cell rating is provided. The charger is fanless, totally quiet, rated at 42V and 2A. Mine measures at 41.8V, which is close enouh and came with sturdy USA spec 3-prong plug and cable.

The front wheel hub on mine came way too tight, the axel was turning rough and difficult. I adjusted it before installing the wheel, and was able to make it turn smoothly and without looseness. If I had left it overtightened, the bearings would probably go bad quickly. The rear feels fine as it is.

The front disk brake caliper was mounted way out of alignment, so it needed to be loosened and aligned with the disk. This is expected, no big deal. The rear disk brake was aligned fairly well.

The disk brakes are not great, as most mechanical cheap 160mm disk brakes are. Probably stop better than a cheap V brake, but nowhere near as well as the good disk brakes on my other bike do (but one of these good brakes costs about 1/3 as much as this entire ebike, so this can be excused). Usually as the disks and pads break-in, the stopping power shoild increase.

There are electric power cutoff switches in the brake levers, so the assist will stop if you try to brake. Cable management is decent, with most wires tucked out of the way well.

If your front light is crooked, like mine was, don't try to force it straight, you will break the plastic. Remove it, then use a screwdriver or hex wrench to twist the mounting bracket to point forward and to eliminate any side to side tilt too.

This bike will work well for tqll folks, in my estimate at least up to 6'5" (195cm). The seat post, at it's tallest setting brings the seat higher than on my full size bike, which is a lot, given I have a 37"+ inseam. At 6'4" I have almost an extra half inch of seat height that I will not be using even at full leg extension. The handlebars can can go higher than the seat by about 5". The distance between the handlebars and seat is just a little shorter than on my mountain bike, so the riding position is very upright.

This is a big (tall) bike, it will not be suitabke for very short people or small kids.
- Mine weights 48lb with battery installed (with fairly light aftermarket platform pedals). Has a very convenient carry handle at the baseof theseat post, so it is easy to carry assembled.
- The top of the seat is 44" from the ground at max. extension (to the maximum mark on the seat post).
- The handlebar height is adjustable, and they can't go very low, lowest is about even with the seat at 44", at the max. height mark is 49", or about 5" above the seat.
- At their highest (seat and handle bars up to max) the riding position is almost fully upright.
- From the center of the top of the seat post horizontally measured to the center of the handlebars tube is 25.5".
- Top of seat to top of pedal is 38.5".
- The bottom bracket is 2" forward of the seat post line.
- From center of BB to top of seat is 32"
- Tire diameter is 22" (set that in the bike computer for accurate speed measurement, mine came default at 20")
- The seat is moderately big, feels comfortable.
- Seatpost diameter I measure at 31.7mm, 54-55cm long.

Why 4 stars?
- The battery pack rattles inside the frame a lot. Will need to put some thick foam or other material to secure it better. Noise aside, the battery moving about will likely cause issues with the electrical contacts. And the added vibration might physically damage it internally.
- The front light might brake if the handlebars are allowed to twist backwards (no mechanical stop to prevent this, the light will hit the frame)
- Poor or missing assembly and use instructions
- Terribly noisy tires (4" knobby tires do that, not u expected, but quite annoying)
- The rims are fairly true side to side, but are somewhat uneven around the area where the rim seam is, so not exactly round, and not sure if this can be easily fixed (or at all).
- The rubber cover on the charge port does not fit and does not stay put.
- No fenders.
- Slight wobble in the steering tube assembly due to the folding mechanism not being super tight.
- The chain slightly rubs the rear tire in 1st gear (the tires are too fatfor where the chain is).

Stay tuned for more.

Review:
The bike:
This appears to be a great little bike. Solid construction, the 7 speed…

7? Yeah, the listing says 6, and I expected twist shifts, but this is a 7 speed index (“trigger”) shift bike.

Where was I? The Shimano 7 speed indexed shifter on this bike is SO superior to the twist shifts available on lower end bikes. My little guy is thrilled at the upgrade. The brake levers are clearly lower end, but they get the job done.

Packaging:
Double packed in two separate cardboard boxes, the bolts on the sides of the wheel STILL managed to poke through the packaging. No apparent damage, but what is going on on the way that they can’t yet manage to avoid destroying bike boxes?

Instructions:
In 2018 I attended a full week of resident training on bicycle maintenance. Worth every minute. I have the tools, I have the training. For me, assembly was trivial - not thanks to the manual, but despite it.

Without my training, I’m afraid that the manual provided - which is intended to cover the assembly of ANY Diamondback bike, mountain, hybrid, kid, adult, etc. - would be about worthless. I’m picturing a single mom trying to give her kid a great bike and finding herself completely out of her depths. All the info is there, but there’s so much extra info in it that it makes it hard to determine exactly what’s relevant unless you already know what you’re doing. And if you already know what you’re doing you don’t need the manual.

Conclusion:
I’d recommend this bike to a friend for their kid. Then I’d assemble it for him/her or recommend they take it to a bike shop to put it together.

First, I bought the 17.5” frame if I recall correctly, which was $490 when I bought it - it’s now listed at ~$630. This bike was rarely worth $490, and that jump is just straight up greed. I’ve put in probably 100+ miles into the bike since I’ve had it, and again the overall build isn’t bad, but if I knew what I knew now, I would just go to the bike store. Review:
For a bike that cost $330 I'm pretty pleased. I'm a 50 year old 6'2" overweight man so I think I'm right in the market demographic for this bike. It arrived quickly. The packaging was slightly damaged. Looks like there was some stress where the axles of the bicycle met the cardboard inside. Fortunately Sixthreezero overpacks everything, so the bike was well protected from damage. Before getting into assembly, note that you will need to pump up the tires before you can ride. It's also helpful to watch some YT videos about assembling these bikes. Also note that the serial number is on a yellow sticker on the outside of the box, so don't throw the box away yet. Note too that the Sixthreezero Forever Warranty is available on their site for possibly less or more money than elsewhere.

Assembly was not extremely difficult. I'm fairly handy, but I don't think the average person needs to pay for assembly. You don't really need extra tools because the bike comes with phillips screwdriver tipped allen wrenches and a multi wrench that fits all the bolts. That said, it might make things easier if you use your own open-ended wrenches and a pair of pliers. The multi wrench hurts your hand if you're really torquing. If you're an older guy there are more things you can do to make assembly easier. First, if you can find a way to elevate the working surface it would make a huge difference. All the crouching while working was difficult. Also you'll want glasses. The text on the instructions is very small. Scissors will help with cutting loose all the packaging, which includes some zip ties. Finally, work somewhere with plenty of light if your bike is black, because it's hard to see the low-contrast parts sometimes. If you're not a fat geezer like me though, no worries! On the technical side I will say there are a few difficult points to the assembly. Make sure to get the front fork the right way around before putting on the handlebars. The brakes go towards the front. Also the handlebars themselves should be positioned with the mounting bar angled forwards and cabling towards the front. The hardest part was attaching the rear fender and rack. The fender attaches in two places on both sides (four total) and it shares the forward mounting points with the rack. I had a devil of a time putting the bolt through the rack and fender mounts and attaching to the right side of the frame. The shift cabling is right there and gets in the way, plus the fender mount seemed a little bent and didn't want to let the bolt go through all the way. Here I used the pliers to bend it a little and give me a little more bolt to work with. One bummer is the nut to attach the front fender was messed up and wouldn't let the bolt go through all the way. I couldn't tighten down the front fender and had to leave it off until I can get another nut. Note that the chain is not on the sprocket and you will have to guide that on while turning the crank. I was wearing gloves and got my finger caught multiple times, so be careful. I also had to adjust the front brakes, which had a bit of play. I did not have to adjust the derailleur like some others had to, but there are instructions for this included.

Once the bike was assembled and the tires pumped up I took a spin. It's a nice ride and feels solid. The shifting worked great. I'm not sure if I maybe need to adjust something, but it does feel like I'm sitting too close to the handlebars. This is odd because the deal with this bike is it's supposed to have a swept-back frame for comfort riding. Another thing is no matter how much I tighten the seat it seems to move while I'm riding. I will admit, I'm pretty heavy, so perhaps that has something to do with it. I'm a little bummed because there are some ugly stickers on the bike that do not come off easily. The pedals and sprocket are marked with L and R so you get the pedals on correctly, but these stickers just shred into tiny bits when you try to get them off. I'll have to take some compound to try and rub them off, and hopefully not mar the finish. There's also a big white "Warning" sticker and "Made in China" right on front of the downtube at the bottom. The kickstand seems a bit small and inadequate. Also it's very tight and squeaks when you kick it down or up. I gave it a shot of WD40, which helped a bit.

Overall I like the bike. It's not a cheapo budget bike, but doesn't cost much more than they do. It's pretty good value for a bike that doesn't cost upwards of $600. Being a large heavy rider further limits the choices, and this bike is pretty good so far. Time will tell.

UPDATE 4/20/2020: I'm still happy with the bike, but I'm finding it needs more adjustment than I originally thought. This is also turning out to be a bit of a nuisance. I am not a bicycle expert by any means, but YouTube videos explain everything one would want to know. I've been having real trouble adjusting the back brakes. They started rubbing and making noise, causing friction, etc. Adjustment should be fairly straightforward according to what I've learned, but no matter what I try it doesn't seem to help. I found out the barrel near the brake lever on the handlebars is bent. I'm not sure now if it was this way when I got the bike, or if something happened. I've been taking great care of the bike and I haven't dropped it on the ground or anything. Given that there was a problem with a different screw right out of the box, I think it was probably just bent to start with. The bottom line is inspect every part of the bike when you get it.

UPDATE July 2000: SixThreeZero customer service has been great. Through no fault of their own, they were forced to be less-than-responsive when I had troubles during the COVID-19 crisis. Since then they have reached out to follow up, and when they found out about my problems they reimbursed me for all I had spent to fix up my bike. I would recommend people inspect their bike when they get it to evaluate whether there are any damaged parts, but then contact 630 customer service as I'm sure they will make it right.

Review:
I’m 5’10, 175lbs.
The bike melts hills but when they get steep, the bike still needs your help with the climb (although not very much) so don’t expect to just use the throttle up the hills. The 300W probably goes up hills with pure throttle no problem.

I got the bike for exercise so this is fine for me.

The front tire was slightly bent on arrival, which I had to true using a rim truing tool I bought.

I have replaced the seat and pedals, as it comes with cheap versions of both. (they had to cut costs to offer this at $650-800) I also added a saddle storage pouch and a phone mount to keep stuff from falling out of my pockets while I ride.

The shock absorbers are decent, and a shock absorbing seat is a great add on for around $30. Woodsy trails are doable, but don’t expect to go rock climbing with it.

The brakes are good, not great, when trying to do a hard stop from 25-30mph. Good luck to you if you accidentally bump the brake rotor while using the bike, it’s white-hot after a few stops. Leaves a cool scar but I don’t recommend it. Maybe a rotor guard would’ve been nice. I wouldn’t have had to reach down to adjust my wheel if it came from the factory straight.

The brakes are still squeaky two months in.

The throttle is limited to about 21mph, but if you pedal hard it is very easy to hit 30mph on this bike. 30mph on the bike feels controlled, but not utterly safe. This isn’t a Tour de France bike, so expect some shimmy at speeds that high. I’ve hit 36mph downhill so far and didn’t really want to go faster on something so light with B- brakes. Having straight wheels out of the box would’ve been awesome, and it was packaged very cleverly, so I’m not sure how the wheel would’ve been bent in transit. Do not yank the bike out of the box, as a previous reviewer showed himself doing just that, then complained about a bent wheel.

Tires are par for the course, better than what comes on most bikes out of the box, and they look more expensive than they are.

Battery lasts forever on a three hour charge, I have yet to kill the battery on a normal 20-30 mile ride. This differs based on how much pedal assist you use. For the best battery life, keep it between 20% and 90%, as this is where batteries like to live for the longest lifespan.

Level one gives you a nice 5mph boost to get rolling.
Level five gets you to 21 mph as fast as the bike can handle.

The motor after two months has started making some noise, but still works. I wear headphones 90% of the time so it doesn’t bother me. The bike is garage kept and not ridden in the rain - I’m the guy that keeps the chain oiled and checks the tire pressure before riding - so why the motor is making noise is beyond me. I’ll take it apart after the warranty and update the review if anything is broken.

Assembly was decent, took about a half hour. Another hour or two tweaking gears, adjustments, and brakes, but I’m picky.

The screen it came with is a different version than shown, but with the same functions.

The gear shifting isn’t clunky, but I wouldn’t call it smooth either. Like any bike, don’t shift it under load. I’ve found it easiest to just leave it at the highest torque setting with just a little pedal assist to get me rolling.

Definitely a value for the price, but makes me wish I got a better model for an extra $1000 somewhere else, or at the very least went with the 300W model for a couple hundred extra.

I got tons of crap from my kid and my significant other for buying this, two months in they both want one as their Walmart bikes they insisted on buying at the same time are falling apart and I can go for much longer rides. (Told ya!)

TL;DR
If you want an eBike under $1000 that will do the job around the trails and suburbs, with maybe a few small modifications to make it more comfy, this is it. If you’re looking to do hardcore mountain biking up expert level slopes on an eBike with pure throttle, save another 1-2k and get a better one or just get an electric dirt bike for a similar price. B+

Review:
It's been 11 months since we bought this tandem monster bike and it's been almost a year of extreme pleasure for us. We love it so much that just like with our dog, we buy little gifts for it. And it's no longer an ''it'' because she is now Agnesaurus rex (Tyranosaurus agnes didn't sit well with the stoker). We bought the bike knowing it's a beach cruiser pumped up with 21-speed gearing so there were no surprises. We knew she won't be a Colorado made-to-fit titanium creation. Anyway, here's our experience with Rexie:

1. Delivery was advanced. It was the biggest and heaviest parcel I've ever received. Inside was a well-padded, partially assembled, gleaming red and black and chrome monstrosity.

2. Assembly was intuitive. I've assembled my growing family's succession of bikes over the years and I consider myself competent by now. I didn't even read the instructions until I read the incredulous reviews about it. I'm keeping the sheet for laughs.

3. I did go to a bike shop! I may be mechanically inclined with all the right tools, but three things I want a pro to do for us: (a) shifting system fine tuning, (b) brake adjustments, and (c) truing the rims. I cannot compromise on these three things because for the very first time, I will be responsible for the safety of a VIP stoker. Read #5 below to see just how VIP she is!

4. Before riding, we researched everything about tandem bikes. We learned in theory how to mount, dismount, how to tackle different terrain and surfaces, and the *very important* communications skills between captain, stoker as well as with other road and trail users. Then, with helmets on, we put theory to practice. One thing I modified from the online instructions: Extra stability and safety during mounting and dismounting are attained if I sit on my crossbar, feet firmly planted to the ground, and brakes applied while the stoker does her preflight ritual, such as plunking herself on her saddle and putting both feet on her pedals..

5. Upgrades and additional accessories: (a) Rear view mirror for stoker - that's her job. (b) Ibera system of rack, saddlebags and trunk. (c) Sunlite front rack. (d) Voyager low riders. (e) Shock absorbing seat post for stoker. (f) Vitesse wider saddle for stoker. (g) Sunlite swing back handlebar for stoker with ergonomic handles. (h) Sunlite adjustable handlebar post for stoker. (i) Schwalbe 1.5''road tires that added speed and reliability. And (j) a brass ding-dong bell for me!!! So you might have surmised by now that we ride the enhanced and upgraded Rexie to other zip codes, camping along the way. Not a single breakdown, not a flat, no incidents at all.

Yes, we're not just happy with out tandem bike, but we have already placed our lives and safety in her hands, I mean, handlebars, and in our Garmin GPS. We highly recommend this bike. It's not the very best money can buy but we're not into competitive or off road riding.

Review:
I have been riding this bike around for the past couple days and I am ready to write my review:

Disclaimer: This is my first e-bike, and the first one I have ever ridden, so I will tailor this review as such and assume this will be either your first or second e-bike purchase or maybe even use. Suffice to say, it may just be easy to impress me.

This is a very enjoyable bike, both on city streets and on trails. I wanted something to play with, and maybe commute to work on sometimes. At 6" 1' tall, I think this is the first bike I've felt I'm not hunched over holding the bars while still being low enough to comfortably touch the ground. The acceleration of the motor is very nice and helps me crossing streets, and I was able to go 24.5mph in max gear with full throttle and pedaling myself. The hydraulic breaks really are a MUST for a bike with this much power. The battery is more than enough for me, either to make it to the office, or on a trail; I wear out before the battery does. The assembly was a little rough but I managed; do NOT adjust the height of the handlebars with the center nut like the manual suggests, but tightening it did re-compress the bearings. I have a few complaints about the bike so far (see below), but the one that I had to remove a star for is the branding. The company name is on virtually every corner, from the cable organizer to the huge white letters on the side. The most egregious is the headlight and taillight, which both feature HEYBIKE illuminated by 3 bright LEDs each, which CANNOT be turned off. I realize LEDs are relatively low-power, but come on... really? You already put your name very largely on the side of the bike, do you need to waste the battery too? I've paid for your product, I don't want to be responsible for advertising as well... I was able to fix this, but still, annoying. Overall it is very fun bike and I'm having a blast, and very reasonably priced for the performance that I got.

Newbie-tip: The electric motor can put out much more power than you can, so at top speed in top gear your pedaling is largely optional; this makes regenerative breaking a little pointless actually, because the amount of energy recovered would be meaningless.

Suggestions: Even though it is designed as a commuter bike, it could be a more comfortable ride. The included city tires get basically 0 traction, which I especially noticed since my first ride after assembling was after a thunderstorm. I suggest riding it to a local bike shop and picking up some more all-terrain tires, as well as a hydraulic bike seat. These things would be nice to have, but obviously would have increased the price point (since I'm paying for them separately), however they really are worth the extra penny I've found.

A programming menu can be accessed by holding + and - on the input pad, and a manual on the options is available on the Heybike website. My top speed was set at 62 by default which makes me think the speed on this may not be limited by software? I would suggest not messing with other settings such as voltage, current or wheel size; I was NOT able to go any faster testing with these for a brief run.

One complaint I had was the photodiode on the headlight, which makes the lights turn on automatically and cannot be turned off with the switch once enabled. Personally I wish it was just excluded completely, because I would like to make the determination on when it is safe to ride without lights. I was able to fix this problem by opening up the headlamp and carefully removing transistor 960 (I think, next to R54, green in photo).

Lastly, lets get to the branding... While we're in the headlamp, I was able to disable the 3 LEDs for the branding there by cutting the traces to R2 with an exacto-knife (red line in photo), it should be pretty easy to see the logic here. I can't help but remark that without the branding, the headlight assembly could be considerably smaller and lighter. For the taillight, I was able to disable all 3 LEDs by simply removing the left one (I think, apologies as I did not take a picture and it is harder to get at the circuit board for this one; the circuit board is a little messier too and I'm not a hardware guy). Its worth noting after doing this things, the display experienced a glitch and I needed to remove the battery completely to reset it; no problems since. I have yet to fix the non-electrical branding on the side, but I am considering either buying black spray paint and taping the section off, or taking it to a car body shop and asking them to paint it.

The last complaint that I can make about the electronics is the tail-light's automatic activation. Don't get me wrong, I find it incredibly handy that the taillight activates and flashes when I press the brake to warn anyone behind me. However I wish it did not happen when the bike was not moving, as I constantly will use the brakes to hold me in place while waiting for a crosswalk or streetlight. In these moments, I wish the taillight wasn't blinking away... I don't want to just disable the blinking feature, so I have yet to come up with a solution for this...

In conclusion, I am very much enjoying my purchase of this bike. I only note all the issues above to help the company improve. If you think you are competent enough to open the electronics, and make some small modifications to suit your likings, then I think I can safely recommend this bike.

Review:
Ok I have a couple of electric bikes and a few mountain bikes. But I wanted one for my wife to enjoy that didn't look like a scooter or and heavy as one too. She needed something to help her keep up with me and the boys. This e-bike from Schwinn was a big hit.

This bike is a light weight electric bicycle and there is a reason its so light too. Its a mountain bike with a small 250watt motor with a removable internal battery. So this is going to be about the weight of a cheeper mountain bike but heavier than a professional one. It works by giving power to the rear motor to push the bike depending on setting forward with every peddle. This is called PAS peddle assist system. If on the more you peddle the more power you get the faster you go. No peddle no power your bike will not move.

PROS:
The battery hold a very decent charge and recharges a bit over 3 hours. We use very little battery power its rarely under 3 bars out of 4. This is made to do most terrain from street to dirt. The tires are too narrow for sand and don't try to drop off a steep drop with it. You do get front and seat shocks that are for light duty. The shifter is a 7 gear twist shift and very very simple for my wife and kids to use. The front and rear brake if adjusted correctly will stop fast as don't show fast wear down. The controls are simple you have power, the amount of power to assist you, and the remaining power. The motor is responsive and you can feel the power kick it with every increase of level.

CONS:
The electronic gages are simple and this may be a sticking point for some. Schwinn does sell gage/control upgrades. The instructions are NOT user friendly. Ive assembled a few bikes in my time and this would require and I recommend taking it to a bike shop for most new riders. The battery is very sleek and discreet often others don't know its a E-bike. Review:
I wanted to put a few thousand miles on this bike before reviewing and feel pretty confident I can give an accurate account of the pros and cons. I bought it as a commuter to work but my commutes involve some distance and climbing so I wanted something sturdy but fairly inexpensive.

Pros:

Cool look
Sturdy frame
Comfortable
Tiagra is good now? I've had a good experience with the groupset
Good commuter if commute is flat

Cons:

Terrible brakes
Incredibly heavy
Value versus price
Paint job is trash and chips if you look at it wrong
Not suitable for serious riding
Performance Bicycles partnership is a joke

It's a bike. And it looks good. Unfortunately it's not a very good bike. Not for $1000. You can get more value at your local bike store in a Giant, Trek, Specialized etc. The brakes are awful and it's very heavy so if you intend on riding off road or doing any climbing you'll expect to make some expensive upgrades to the brakes and wheel set. This won't change the fact that this is one of the heaviest aluminum frames I've ever ridden. Aluminum has come a long way over the years but Tommaso hasn't gotten the memo. I use it as a commuter but tend to get about 2000ft climbing between work and back. The breaks are not intended for more than cruising around town. Certainly not for gravel riding as it's intended. I've had significant issues with the brakes. I was sceptical anyway but found that shipping to Performance Bicycles to have assembled was a joke. I had to take it to my bike shop to have everything redone. Avoid this option. They don't care and their mechanics are terrible. Then the paint job. It looks cool, at first. I have a dozen "big brand" bicycles and mostly high end $3000 -$6000 but even of the cheaper more casual rides I have the paint has never chipped or come off like this. The Tommaso's paint may be it's worst drawback. It's so bad a brake cable near the hesdtube has literally worn the paint to the metal just from turning the handlebars.

At the end of the day this bike is not a great value. You're not going to get the support of buying a new bike from your FLBS and you can do more with $1000. I was curious and took a chance but do regret not investing the money in something else.

Review:
Bought this bike for ease of transportation to and from my job which was a town over, a few months ago after having finally received my tax return as I can't afford to pay for an actual car. I apologize in advance for the lengthy review but I wish to warn potential buyers in detail about what they're getting.

It arrived quickly and intact, wasn't all too hard to put together despite some slightly confusing things which many other reviews have gone into detail about already...

At first I thought I had a gem of a bike after getting everything set up and figuring out all the controls, et cetera. To it's credit the battery has a good bit of capacity to it and the motor is capable of kicking out around like 20 mp/h or more depending on what you're on and if you're pedaling or not.

But moving on to the HUGE problems I've had with this bike, everything worked fine for the first week before I learned that this bike's got some really cheap, poorly manufactured parts.

Within the first week and a half or so, the locking mechanism for the bike battery somehow inexplicably completely broke, the key lock mechanism quite literally fell out of the slot entirely, leaving only the locking metal pin to keep the battery in place.

Additionally within a week after that, the seat that came with this bike actually completely broke off of the post upon hitting a very small pothole on the road in the middle of the night on a freeway, leaving me to have to ride ~6 more miles back home standing up... Not cool. (I'm 5'10 and 210 lbs for the record... I'm a tad on the heavy side but that's still ridiculous for how easily it broke!)

I had thought that this could have been a simple fluke in manufacturing with these parts and contacted support for this company to order replacements (which by the way is operated by Chinese people using a translator so there's a slight language barrier at play)

Replacements for the battery locking mechanism and a new seat arrived about a week and a half after several days' worth of back and forth with support to try and explain my problem exactly so I can get replacements.

Alas, I kid you not, within three whole days of very light, bump free riding, the new battery lock broke in the EXACT SAME WAY. The seat seems to be holding up but that's a moot point considering major problem #2 which I'm now dealing with.

After a combined total of like two and a half months of riding this bike with a conscious effort to avoid potholes across perhaps ~200-300 miles for a grand total I've ridden, several spokes on the back wheel suddenly break all within the same day, counting at least five spokes broken and at least 3 more damaged.

I contacted support to ask for a replacement wheel since I lack the tools/cash, physical ability or knowledge to repair a wheel with broken spokes but they were extremely ADAMANT on only sending me replacement spokes which I can't use. I had to get a hold of a local professional to attempt to get help in fixing this, and even with his tools, it was beyond his ability to fix because the cheapo tires they use bent pretty easily...

I'm now looking at having to spend around 150-200 dollars out of pocket simply to buy a new wheel and get the motor hub transferred on to a new rim with new spokes because of shoddy manufacturing, and I can barely afford my rent as it is... Pretty awesome.

I'd suggest steering FAR clear of this bike if you don't know much about bike repair because you may end up in my situation as well.

Review:
These days, it's cheaper to buy a complete bike than to buy a frame & fork set. So... I set out looking for a bike that had what I wanted at the cheapest price. I'm a hefty guy, so no carbon fiber for me... which means Throne and Cyborg are a no go. I wanted a thicker styled frame in 100% 6061 alloy. It came down to Golden and 6ku. 6ku has a decent reputation at this price point, 6ku won.

HINT HINT: I strongly urge you to check out 6ku's website to see additional tech specs before purchasing.

Fast forward, the bike arrives, well packaged. The frame is well built, the tires are blah... standard issue Kenda tires with Kenda tubes. The Tektro breaks, again blah... actually my front break had a bad paint job, but all else was functional. The rims are OK, but the back rim is slightly out-of-round, which my local shop fixed up for me. Also the bearing nuts were way too tight out-of-box and not adequately lubricated. I fixed that... The chain is cheap and will stretch quickly (see above where I mention that I'm hefty) but it will do for now. 1 of the hex nuts for the rear wheel was stripped, out of box; luckily I had spares. The plastic pedals are a joke, I bought some really nice platform pedals on Amazon with spd clips on 1 side.

I bought this bike for the frame, mostly, so for that It did it's job. I replaced the tires and tubes (Vittoria hybrid road tires, 700x28c pictured), but kept the rims. I replaced the tektro brake levers with TT break levers from Soma. I replaced their handle bars with a T2 wing bullhead handle bar, 44cm width, very nice.... I've kept the seat for now, but it's not great and I'll replace it eventually. Also, I've seen plenty of complaints about the BB breaking,so I'm gearing up to replace that as well.

That said, I'm happy with my purchase. All in all, I got what I wanted for about $600, which is a few hundred less than the starter Throne or CYBORG, which I would still have had to modify.
