Review:
To say I'm pissed off about this bike/purchase, it would be a severe understatement. Thus far, this review has no bearing on the actual quality of the bike, but the condition in which I received it and the decision making (or lack thereof) in regards to stickers. I'm well aware that this isn't $5k bike, but these issues have nothing to do with quality of components. Keep in mind for the things I'm discussing, I purchased two different bikes from DiamondBack, this being one. Problems were nearly identical between the two.

1) The axle lock-nuts were so tight that the wheels would only rotate for a couple revolutions with a decent hand spin. I'm no bike expert, but I knew something was up. When I removed the wheels to inspect the bearings, I could barely spin the axle with my fingers. It felt like the bearings were so compressed that if I attempted to ride it, I would've destroyed them *and* the race (or whatever it's called that they sit in) within minutes. How could a professional bike company set up an axle like this... or 4 of them?

2) Missing a couple hub seals. No big deal, but I can't find replacements online. There doesn't seem to be a standard naming convention and the ones I've found look slightly different.

3) Discs were engaging almost non-stop. As I'm not an highly experienced, this took some time to move the brake calipers around and adjust the backside pad by itself to get it just right. However, the bigger problem was the fact that the rotor itself was warped slightly. 3 out of 4 wheels had significant contact (2 bikes) with the disc pads either non-stop or because they were warped. The boxes were in good condition and the rotors weren't touching anything. How were almost all warped?

4) Only 2 out of the 4 wheels (2 bikes) would be considered true. One on each bike had at least one wheel that was either horizontally or vertically out of alignment (or both). They aren't horrible, just worth noting. Most people I think will just blindly ride the bike out of the box.

5) This is what truly pissed me off about this bike: The fking stickers. Not only are there an no less than ~25 of these fking things on each bike, but the choice of glue is asinine at best. Most of the stickers, while a pain to remove, came off without too much effort and left no glue behind. The same cannot be said about the fking stickers on the wheels. Did you know that this bike has 27.5" rims that are double-walled aluminum? Well, fear not, regardless of the angle you are looking at the bike, you will be reminded by EIGHT fking stickers on the rims telling you this from every single fking angle. Oh, you don't like them? Hell, just remove them like the rest! Nope. The glue is some sort of alien super compound that THREE DIFFERENT BRANDS of "goo off" styled sticker/glue remover would barely touch. I even tried a blow-dryer. Nothing makes this tar-like substance come off the fking rim. I several hours just getting the front rim ALONE done and it's not even done. I tried heat, plastic scraping tools, glue emulsifiers, paper towels, cloth rags, old shirts, pieces of jeans, and finally fking Scotch-Brite pads. It took HOURS to do one wheel poorly. And for the record, I'm 220lbs and leg press 1k. I have a fairly strong grip.

The fking moron at the company who thought it was a good idea to put those stupid fking things and use that fking glue should be immediately fired as this will ABSOLUTELY be the last DB bike I ever buy. Imagine buying a new car and then you find out the dashboard is covered in tar. You'd ask yourself, "why did they put this here? What kind of moron would think this okay?" That's the equivalent.

The rest of the actual bike seems to be good so far, but it's REALLY hard looking past the other things. They matter just as much to me. If they don't to you has a prospective buyer, then great.

As an an ending side note, they don't publish negative reviews on their site.

Review:
I biked about 2k miles last year with my Walmart $100 MTB, mostly on a paved trail. I bought this road bike about 2 weeks ago and had about 120 miles on it. So far I am neither happy or unhappy with it. Here are my initial thoughts on this bike:
Pros:
1. It is a lighter bike than my MTB, though it is still about 30lbs. Tires are thinner and can be inflated up to 85psi. All these result roughly 10% gain on speed with less effort to pedal compared to my MTB.
2. Dropped handle bar gives you more options to position yourself against the strong wind.
3. Easy to assemble. I just need to true the wheels and adjust the brakes and shifters.
Cons:
1. Seat is not comfortable especially during a long bumpy ride.
2. No bottle holder or threaded holes for one. You need to buy the holder separately along with a tap bit.
3. The derailleur shifters are mounted on the stem. It is not that practical if you need to shift constantly.
4. The front derailleur shifter does not have “catching mechanism”. It is like a linear pull where you have to estimate the catching positions of each of those three front gear rings. Luckily I don’t need to shift it that often.
5. Tech support wasn’t available at the time I called two weeks ago. I left my phone number and have not got a call-back.

Bottom line: It is a great cheap bike for commuting on a flat road. If you bike to exercise, you might need to ride a little bit longer to burn the same amount of calories than on a heavier bike.

Review:
I like to give reviews early to give my first impressions of a product. First of all, this is packed very well, so chances of damage in shipping seem minimal. (Mine had no damage.) I had a little trouble getting it out of the box, as everything is hooked together with plastic zip ties. The black color that I got is gorgeous and very classy looking. I haven't gotten it assembled yet, as there are a number of things to attach (front fender, front wheel, pedals, seat and front tire). Assembly is a little challenging and I had problems even though I am usually good at assembling things. One thing that stopped me from putting it together is that the manual recommends you use a lithium based grease on moving parts when you assemble. I had no grease at all, so picked up some from a bike shop. I learned something important from the bike shop. DO NOT use lithium based grease recommended in the manual if you live in a very hot dry climate. It will dry too much and lock up the wheels of the bike. Other places where it is colder or with more humidity, it works fine. The grease that I got is called Polylube 1000 Polyurea Grease. The manual also confused me about the brakes as it describes brake cables, but I discovered that this model uses coaster brakes, so there are no cables. (Apparently they wrote one manual for several different models of bikes.) I am glad for the coaster brakes, as I learned to ride a bike with coaster brakes. I never liked hand cable brakes, as it always seemed at some point the cable would break or brakes always needing adjustment. Note that I got the single speed model and it should be perfect for me. Seems ideal for casual flatland riding, which is what I plan to use it for. Now I just need to get a helmet and bicycle pump. The tires do come inflated, but not sufficiently. Update: I got the bike together, sort of, but the front fender was not positioned correctly. Also had a big problem with the seat post. Be very careful to make sure the seat post is attached to the seat before you insert the post into the frame. I dropped the post into the frame and it dropped in so far that the seat would not attach to it and I couldn't get it out again. BE VERY CAREFUL about this.
I ended up taking this to a bike shop and they got it out and attached and adjusted the seat; adjusted the handlebars and inflated the tires to the correct pressure. I also had trouble mounting the front fender, which I had mounted wrong; they fixed that too. They also adjusted the chain, which was a little too tight out of the box. They tried to adjust the back fender, but the screws holding it were cranked in so tight that they would not move. A word about the grease. Grease is only inside sealed bearings and you can't get to them without special tools. The bike has proper lubrication out of the box, so only after some use and some time would you need to lubricate it. The one place I did use grease is on the threads on the pedals when attaching them and the bike shop confirmed that was the right thing to do. Unless you are really familiar with bike mechanics, best to get some professional help on this to make sure everything is good. I should knock off a star or two from my rating for the problems I had and the confusing manual, but it is such a nice bike that I am staying with the 5-star rating.

Review:
I have owned Ebikes since 2011. This is the first time ordering this particular brand. What caught my eye is that the foot pegs are placed where pedal usually go, rather than located on the front wheel spokes, (where you have to reach your legs forward), so someone short like me can reach them; and it can fold to fit in a small trunk.

I was unable to find the app in google play and the manual didn't mention anything about it. Apart from that, this bike is heavier than advertised by about 8 pounds, but it's solid, and well built with a closed motor case to allow you to ride in inclement weather. Because these batteries cannot be purchased or swapped out, I do want to provide some helpful tips to prolong the life of your battery. Do not store the bike in your car or outside when temps are very cold/hot. Doing so will guarantee a dead battery within a year.

Do not ever charge the battery without allowing bike to cool down first; meaning, never charge immediately after riding, let the bike sit for at least 30 minutes. Except for the very first charge, never allow the battery to charge to 100% unless you will use within 15-30 minutes. Only charge to 100% on rare occasions if absolutely necessary. Never, store the bike in a hot or freezing garage. Never, ever, ever store the bike at a 100% charge. Always store between 25-30% to 70% max. I promise you, this will greatly extend the life of your battery. When storing (preferably indoors) you only need to check the battery once every two months, and then top off the charge if needed. I repeat, never charge to 100% on the top off.

Unless battery is very low, check the bike every 15 minutes when charging. When charging/unplugging; plug the cord into bike before the wall, and unplug from the wall, before the bike after charging. Please note, except for brakes and tires etc, this bike cannot be repaired. Bike shops cannot get parts. Ebike shops will not work on them because they are meant to be disposable. Please allow the battery to drop to 20% before charging and charge only to 80%. This will provide you about 1000 charges on the same battery before the battery is no longer able to keep a charge.

You might think I am silly, but I have extended the life of all my bikes years beyond the manufactures warnings. This bike is fantastic on flat road and slight hills, but does not have the torque for big hills. This bike far exceeds the Swagtron in every way; including tire size. In closing, the first thing I did was swap the seat. No matter how tiny you are, the seat is uncomfortable even on the shortest ride. The seat I got looks like two butt cheeks, and is very comfy. I don't have phone or would post a photo of seat. Just type in big butt bike seats and there are a ton of great choices all reasonably priced. Happy riding! You will not be disappointed in this bike. Review:
[[VIDEOID:3c004b4915fc69f9dffa751eff71206c]] Short Version: Super light weight and so smooth with the Grease-free, maintenance-free belt.

Long Version:
As beautiful as it is functional, it is a modern marvel of bicycle engineering in a pint-size package. From its hand-brushed and lacquered aluminum frame to its belt drive, it leaves kids begging for more while their parents simply stare in awe. Fully loaded with 16″ air tires on aluminum rims, front and rear V-pull brakes (no coaster brake!) and a remarkable grease-free, maintenance-free belt drive, weighs in at about 13.7 lbs., about 10 lbs. less than most lower-end 16″ bikes. With a minimum seat height of 19″, is the perfect first pedal bike for any balance bike graduate.
While the brushed aluminum frame steals the show, the belt drive is the icing on the cake. In addition to being grease and maintenance-free, the belt essentially prevents any snags on clothing and, unlike a chain, will not stretch or easily slip off the gears.
Another main draw is the lack of a coaster brake. Required by the CPSC on all bikes with a minimum seat height of less than 16″, coaster brake often cause more harm than good for graduates of balance bikes who are accustom to hand brakes. While learning to pedal, many kids accidentally pedal backwards. On a bike with a coaster brake, pedaling backwards causes the bike to stop abruptly, causes them to lose all their momentum, while a bike without a coaster brake is much more forgiving and keeps moving forward. Instead of a coaster brake, it has two short-reach, front and rear, V-pull brakes.

My 4yrs old is riding it an hr daily. I will continue to update this review.

Update 5/18/20: I've a chance to compare it to a Woom 3. The gear ratio on the Woom is very low. Kids can't go fast on the Woom. The components on the Woom are much smaller and lower quality, the chain is noisy and always rubbing the guard, the guard is flimsy, thin, moving around as you ride, it's not screwed to the frame, just sitting on the chain. While 2lb lighter is great, until I realize where they cut corners and use cheap parts. All the parts on the Belsize are from brand names; Continental belt, Kenda tires, Tektro brakes. The Flat handlebar on the Belsize is probably too aggressive for kids under 5, it forces the kid to lean forward too much. The good news is that it's a 1" standard size, and you can replace it for around $20. Kids sit a lot more upright on the Woom 3.

Update July 2021: It looks like they addressed the biggest flaw. I see that the 2021 version has a Riser Handlebar, much better than the Flat one, but still on the aggressive side, perfect as a mountain bike though. Too bad, my son won't have this new version to test because he is now super happy with a Woom 3. He stopped using the 2020 version since last summer because of the bad Flat handlebar design.

Review:
I will start by saying that I love my Eahora XC100. I love the way its style and design are far more attractive than many of the boxy, more expensive models available. I get many compliments on it. Since I only want to use it for pedal assist on roads or paved trails I find its power and performance are plenty for me. HOWEVER, if you buy this bike know the risk you are taking by buying directly from a foreign manufacturer. While I believe Eahora customer service has a positive attitude and desire to please the customer, if your bike has a problem it will be costlier in terms of both time and money to have it fixed, even if it is under warranty.

Riding my bike in May 2021 it stopped working and flashed an error message on the screen. I am not very handy, so I called around to find a bike shop to diagnose the problem. Out of five or so shops I called, only one said they would take a look at it. The other shops only serviced e-bike brands they sell or bikes that use the same powertrain as those they sell. It took 4 months of back and forth emails among me, my bike shop and Eahora to finally diagnose the problem - a faulty controller. I am sure the delays can be attributed both to Eahora as well as my bike shop as they have been slammed with repair requests over the summer. Once Eahora finally agreed that the controller needed to be replaced, I still had to pay to ship the part from China (over $60) even though the bike was under warranty when it broke. On top of that I had to pay the bike shop over $320 for the diagnosis and repairs since the warranty only covers parts.

I am happy to report that the repairs were successful and the bike seems to be performing better than ever, leading me to suspect the controller was faulty all along before it finally died. As long as the bike continues to perform well I will still feel I have gotten a good value, despite the extra cost and loss of 4 months of use. However, I personally will not take the same risk if I buy another e-bike. I would only purchase a bike from a dealer or manufacturer who can provide local warranty repair that covers both parts and labor. If Eahora were able to make arrangements for this kind of service in my local area, I would not hesitate to buy Eahora again.

Review:
At first, the power and quickness of the electrical assist surprised me, but I got comfortable in no time. I hate to admit it, but I find myself using the electric mode (which requires no pedaling) more and more everyday. It is much like a scooter and very fun. Overall the bike handles like a cruiser and pedals with ease given 7 gear options. The shifter works well and does not get hung up too often. 

The bike is heavier with the battery but it is not that noticeable. The battery can also be removed when you know you won't be using it, or when you're charging it. It is GREAT that this has disc brakes to slow down the power of an electric bike. I kept track and for over one week, 1 hr/day, ~15 miles using assist and electric only mode, the battery indicator shows half life. It folds down to a more compact size, which is so useful if you want to transport it in your car, or fold it up for storage.  We got this initially for grandma to be able to keep up with the kids.  It turned out to be too high for her legs at the lowest setting (she's 5'1"").  My wife (5'4"") has no issues and loves using this bike with the kids. Overall, we never expected to be so won over by electric bikes; this is a great ride, and at a great price for what you're getting. There are other 'bells and whistles' included like a very loud alarm and front/back lights/accessories that add to overall biking safety and comfort.

Unboxing the bicycle was easy and the package included all the tools needed for assembly. It took about 30 minutes to put together (handle bars, seat, front wheel, fenders, pedals, air pumped into tires). There was no instruction manual in the box and the QR code led to nowhere, but I was able to find how-to videos on other similar models.  I also later found that they emailed me some tips, which were helpful.  Speaking of the seller, we contacted them because of an issue with the battery and they resolved it quickly; we were happy to see that they offered good customer service. Would be a perfect commuter's bike.

Review:
UPDATE, November 2021. Earlier this year (in June) I was pedaling my way up a hill using motor assist when the bike just stopped. The lights were still on, everything looked like it should work, but it didn't.

That's when I entered a Kafkaesque nightmare of pain and suffering. First, I contacted the seller, who sent endless requests for me to send pictures and videos of what was going on. Even when I did, more requests came. This lasted for well over a month. At this point, the seller advised me to take it to a bike shop and get it fixed and they would reimburse me. No way was I going to do that.

So, I contacted Amazon, thinking the matter would be resolved rather quickly. No dice. Amazon refused to do anything, even though the seller had clearly advertised a six month warranty and the malfunction fell within that. They kept promising to do an A-Z claim, but then kept saying I needed to wait 48 hours. When I would come back after 48 hours, they would claim that I needed to wait 48 MORE hours. This also went on for months. Nobody at Amazon every solved my problem, despite all I've heard and experienced regarding Amazon's spectacular customer service.

One Amazon rep suggested I contact the manufacturer. So, I did. And guess what? The manufacturer's contact info was exactly the same as what the seller sent me. They were the same person. LOL. Can't make this up. And virtually every seller of Vivi bikes listed showed the same information. Unreal.

So, I went back to bugging the seller. At one point, he offered to take the bike back for a full refund, if I paid to have it shipped. To China. Literally, that would have been half the cost of the bicycle. So, I refused that, obviously.

Finally, in OCTOBER, after having missed half the summer and a large portion of fall riding, the seller agreed to refund $200 and send me a new motor controller in an attempt to fix it. I got the $200 refunded to my credit card, but the motor controller hasn't arrived yet (on a slow boat from China, no doubt, if it's coming at all).

So, I've been calling around to see if someone locally can fix my Chinese e-bike. Turns out, nobody will even look at it. So, if I ever get the motor controller (not holding my breath) I will be on my own getting it wired up and hope that this fixes the problem. If I install it correctly, that is. Maybe I will, maybe not. Who knows.

So, if you're thinking about getting one of these, buy a cheap standard non electric bike for $150 or so, flush $200 down the toilet, and take $200 out of your account for a few months and put it back in, and it will be a less frustrating approximation of my situation as it stands right now.

I'll be back if the seller sends the motor controller. In other words, I probably won't be back.

ORIGINAL REVIEW FOLLOWS.

First, some background.

Last year, a buddy of mine talked me into going on a bike trip. I pulled my 25 year old mountain bike out of storage. It was in not-so-good shape. I put a little money, time and elbow grease into it and got it ready for the trip. Except for one big hill, I enjoyed that trip more than I ever thought I would.

Ever since, I began thinking that a little help would make the ride that much more enjoyable. So, I started researching ebikes. My first thought was to buy a kit and install it on my old bike (kinda like those people who put flashy rims on a 1995 beater car), but I decided to skip the hassle and complication, and for a few (hundred) dollars more, get this from Amazon.

About me: I am pushing 50. I am not, nor have I ever been, a "mountain biker". I am not "extreme" nor "gnarly". I can't recall ever being "stoked". I don't refer to people as "dudes". I avoid energy drinks, don't wear spandex, and am not "extreme" in any sense of the word. I just wanted something that would help me to enjoy riding a bike without requiring me to wear myself out.

Once the bike arrived, my helper (pictured above) and I set out to begin assembly. There is nothing difficult about assembly, but the directions were somewhat confusing. For example, it said to set the fork of the bike so that the caliper was facing forward. This being the first disc brake bike I owned, I didn't understand what a forward or backward caliper looked like. After a little detective work, I figured it out. A better way of putting it would be, "Set the fork so that the caliper is on the same side of the bike that it is on the rear brake." That would make far better sense.

Despite this, the manual was NOT written in broken English. Everything was understandable from a linguistic standpoint. Some of the pictures and illustrations were of other bikes, but they were still useful, if somewhat small and lacking detail.

Everything else was straightforward. I started looking at the bike and evaluating it before I took my first ride (battery was still charging).

Things I liked and disliked to this point:

Finish is excellent. It's not high gloss, which is fine (that's the style these days). Everything looks powder-coated, nice and even. Welds are neat and solid. The seat wasn't bad, but I replaced it with a fat-boy seat anyway. Pedals are plastic, seem sturdy enough, but I'd like alloy.

Hardware: Most of it looks good, but the retaining pin for the front wheel screws on with a plastic nut, which I do NOT like. I may attempt to find a metric wing nut and washer in the same size and replace it. I just don't trust plastic hardware, and it seems a lot to ask from a piece of plastic to hold the front wheel on. Nevertheless, I haven't had any issues with it in the short time I've ridden the bike.

Appearance: I had considered the Ancheer in the same price range, but it looks like an old man's bike (said the almost 50 year old man). This looks way better than that. It has a blackout treatment on the wheels, appropriately knobby tires, modern looking color scheme and graphics, and just an all around look of quality. Not that the Ancheer isn't, but I much prefer the appearance of this. The down tube is over-sized and squared, which adds strength, but it just looks good too.

Tool kit: You get a multi-use bike wrench/Phillips screwdriver, several Allen wrenches, and a double ended two-sized wrench that looks like it was cast in someone's backyard, not forged, complete with flashing around the outside edge. They're functional, if not the highest quality. I used them a little to assemble and adjust the bike and they worked fine. I put them in a pouch which I attached to the bike, and will keep them there in case they are needed.

Battery: Can charge on or off the bike. I just use the key (don't forget to find this in the box, VERY important) to remove the battery, take it in the house, and charge it. The key does NOT enable or disable the battery. It simply locks the battery to the bike to prevent theft. There is a switch on the opposite side that turns the battery on and off, as well as a charging jack with a rubber cover to keep dirt out. The whole setup is very slick and works well. I charged the battery with the switch in both on and off position, and it didn't seem to make any difference. Also, there's a meter on the side of the battery that indicates charge when you push a button.

First ride: To start, the brakes needed some adjustment, which I did at the brake levers by turning the small adjusters where the cables came out. The brakes have a curious tendency: when going down a long hill, if you apply the brakes evenly, without increasing or decreasing pressure on the levers, it will feel like the brakes are a bit inadequate. But, after a short time, they will "heat up" and begin to grip better. There will be a noticeable "slow down" a few seconds after applying the brakes. This can be disconcerting if you're not prepared for it.

Also, the more I rode, the more the rear caliper made noise, even when I wasn't braking. It might need adjusted a bit more, or the pads may need scuffed, or both. Regardless, it's a minor issue.

What wasn't a minor issue was how far out of adjustment the derailleurs were. The front was so far out that I shifted down once and the chain came off completely. I wasn't far from home, so I just limped back in throttle mode (electric to the rescue!). I adjusted the limiter screws until they lined up correctly and haven't had a problem since. The rear was better, in that the chain never jumped off, but it occasionally "slips" a gear while pedaling. It helps to move the shift lever up or down a notch to make sure the derailleur lines up correctly over the sprocket. I still need to adjust this a little more for it to be perfect.

As far as the ride is concerned, I replaced the seat with a suspension seat made for fat boys like me, which really smooths out the bumps. The tires are rated for 45-60 PSI, and I only inflated to 45. This probably hurts my battery range, but it makes for a comfortable ride and slightly better grip on loose surfaces. I may compromise and set it at 50 or so. I figured the front shock would be a gimmick, but it really does absorb a lot of vibration and bumpiness and makes the ride much less fatiguing.

Electric power is nice. In my area, there are lots of hills. The motor won't take me up hills on throttle only, but it makes it easy to pedal up them. 250 watts equates to about 1/3 of a horsepower, so keep your expectations realistic and you won't be disappointed. This is an assistive motor more than one that does the work for you. That said, the only time I pedaled was when it seemed like I would lose sufficient momentum that my speed would drop below 10 mph. My last ride had elevation changes of over 100 feet, and grades as steep as 7%. I was able to pedal up them with minimal-to-moderate effort. I would classify my "in-shape" level as better than "Little Debbie Corp. sends me a Christmas card every year" but not quite as good as, "Doesn't huff and puff after walking up a flight of stairs".

Nevertheless, I rode for well over an hour on this thing, up and down hills, big stupid grin on my face, still getting some exercise, and only came home because it was getting dark (I set out to run the battery down and failed). You can buy more powerful bikes, but you'll probably have to go up a couple hundred dollars, and for me, it's worth the savings to pedaling a little bit, since I could use the activity anyway.

That said, on flat, level ground, the thing will move even fat boys along at a brisk pace. I could easily hit 18 mph (GPS confirmed) on throttle only on level ground, depending on whether the wind was at my back or I was driving straight into it. Either way, the bike moved along briskly without feeling unsafe. If you live in an area where the land is almost completely flat, you could do lots of local commuting with this thing, not having to pedal a bit. You can go up small grades with throttle mode only, and if things steepen up, you can pedal once or twice to keep the momentum up. In all, I rode about 7 miles on my first "real" ride on this bike and while I did get some exercise, I wasn't sore, wrung out, or exhausted when I got home. Perfect.

Pedal assist mode is interesting if you've never ridden a bike like this before. You start pedaling, and think, "This thing isn't working at all." Then all of a sudden, the pedals get really light and you surge forward. There were three levels to pedal assist, and I always used the highest level. It can be a bit disconcerting, because sometimes the motor doesn't shut off immediately when you stop pedaling. Squeezing the brakes seems to stop the motor, though.

About the only thing I can see that I DON'T like concerning the electric assist is that it's hard going from pedal assist to throttle mode. Depending on which level of PA you're in, you might have to hit the button 3X before it switches (it's sequential). In addition to changing gears, it can be a bit like driving a dual stick 18 wheeler...lol.

On the last leg of the journey, I hit another flat and switched to throttle mode, and confirmed that the top speed was still the same, meaning the battery wasn't significantly down on power after going 7 miles. The battery meter bobbed between 2-3 bars out of 5, which suggested that the battery was somewhere around half charged. This would put the range (for me) at about 14 miles, which is more than adequate considering the hills I was riding up and the extensive use of throttle-only in pretty much any situation that I could do it. Again, I set out to drain the battery and after over an hour of going up and down hills using pedal assist and riding throttle-only, I failed to do it.

Stability is great. At one point, i was blasting down a paved road at full throttle when, lo and behold, the pavement ended and it turned to slightly-smaller-than-golf-ball-sized gravel. I was afraid I was going to wipe out, but the bike was very composed (largely due to the front shock, I imagine) and didn't show any signs of sliding or tipping. I was able to apply the brakes and get the speed down safely and quickly without issue.

All in all, a very nice bike for the price, and thus far, I haven't seen anything about it that gives me second thoughts about my purchase. Keep in mind, this review was written in Week One, so your mileage may vary.

This is a long-term review and I will come back in a few months with updates about range, ruggedness, wear, etc.

I do have a concern that has nothing to do with the bike itself. Vivi sent me a card for a "$40 discount" if I put a 5 star review on Amazon, took a screenshot, and sent it to them.

Needless to say, I passed on that. Am I the only person who got this? Unfortunately, if people really did give this bike 5 stars, that practice certainly diminishes the reliability of the ratings.

Also, I am not listed as a "verified purchaser" because I bought this under a different listing, and reviewing for that has been shut down due to "unusual activity". Probably because of the $40 discount given for a 5 star rating, lol.

Thus far, the bike has been very good and I would buy it again without reservation.

Review:
(Bought this bike on a different family account for free shipping at the time. )

What to say you know? Two years of experiences with this bike. There are other options on Amazon for this price point now but I doubt any of them could beat out the experience I had with this model. The bike I received was never lacking in performance and has taken an enormous amount of abuse from an inexperienced biker. This was my main method of transportation daily off and on for a period of two years plus. At the height of use I was riding this bike 100 miles a week for a period of about three months straight. I may be looking to upgrade soon but it is still effective and I will continue to ride it till I upgrade.

-It has comparable weight for other bikes of this price point.
-The 21 speed felt effective to me. Eventually I was biking at the top/hardest gear with continued effort but that was after a year plus heavy riding.
-The brakes got a bit wonky 1 year+ into it. Needed to replace the brake pads at a reasonable point but could never quite calibrate them perfectly after that, resulting in a reduction of efficiency. This is most likely due to me riding the bike hard but not cleaning any mechanical components relating to the brake mechanisms.
-Had many flats on the back tire but now I suspect this is due to me riding way under the recommended PSI constantly. In addition to that I frequent freeways with excess debris.
-Never replaced the chain and the crank/pedal assembly seems loose. It kinda wobbles a bit when peddling. This has led to the wear and tear of the protective metal pieces on the outside of the chain/pedal area breaking and me subsequently cutting of the remaining metal. This could probably be avoided by getting proper maintenance on the bike at a local shop, which I never did.

Review:
This bike has turned out to be a very good purchase for me.

I live on my boat in Los Angles and am able to attend to 90% of my brick and mortar shopping without using my car since this bike is beefy and has no problem handling a couple of saddle bag type baskets as well as a basket on the handlebars. A 36 pack of canned beer rides securely on the rear rack held in place with bungee cords

I bought the three speed model and am glad I did. Even though the area around us is pretty flat there are a few sloped ramps, on our great local bike paths, that make me appreciate the ability to shift down. Down wind on a level surface, or down hill, the high gear is useful. Some days the breeze off the ocean is strong enough to cause me to shift down when headed up wind. The three speed has no derailleur so the bike has a chain guard.

This bike is very easy to ride and takes a lot of the back and hand stress out of riding my bike. Im 72 and outgrew dropped handlebars about half a century ago.

It took me a few days to get used to coaster brakes again, after decades of cool bikes with hand brakes. But now Im cool with the coaster brake and really like the lack of clutter on the handle bars.

I added a bell, lights and a holder for my smart phone. I also added a really nice rear view mirror which is a great safety feature. I got a nice beefy lock on Amazon and really like the fact that I can drop it in my basket instead of going to the trouble of installing it on the mount on the bike every time I take off.

Since I live in southern California fenders seemed pointless so I skipped that accessory.

The bike is easy to ride with its big tires but is not fast. If you want a fast bike a beach cruiser is probably not what you should buy.

Unless I have some compelling reason to get in my car I do all my local travel on my bike. Its easier, faster many times, and there are no parking hassles or cost. I rode it 25 miles round trip to a doctor appointment a week ago. It was along the beach where there is a nice bike path and lots of scenery. It was not an exhausting experience but then I was not in a big hurry.

As I ride to the gym every morning Im passed by cyclists on high tech bikes who are bent into incredibly uncomfortable looking positions over their dropped handle bars. As they zoom past I reflect on the fact that I definitely bought the right bike for me and also that some people should not be wearing lycra cycling outfits.

The only negative about this purchase was that the packaging on the bike was not adequate to protect it in shipment. The three speed shifter on the rear axel had broken through the cardboard box and got scratched up in shipment. The damage did not look like it was more than cosmetic and I did not want o hassle with repacking the bike to return it so I went ahead and accepted as it was.

Review:
Asked for them to trade this out for their Spark model, got this one instead after contacting the seller to ask for either a refund or the other version, which they said was alright. When delivery (and free time) showed up, I discovered it was. in fact, this bike. I have yet to ride the bike as I am beyond dead tired as of writing this review, but the thing came less assembled than you would think, namely the front brakes that came with mine were completely unset, and there was no included hex wrench to allow me to fix this glaring issue. The included, hardwired headlight feels super cheap, attaches nowhere to the included wire basket, has no fixed mount on the front of the bike, and, as mentioned is hardwired. Overall, I feel rather cheated and would recommend going with something else unless you really want to spend almost $500 on something incredibly mediocre.

edit1: After having a days rest, and mounting the headlamp to my cup holder now at the front of the thing, I can say it's a good bike once you get it fully assembled. The spring they used on the front brake to keep it from rubbing on the wheel constantly is a little weak and required a bit of extra tweaking to get right. Gear shifting is a little backwards at first, but is smart for how it is set up. The light is good, but the horn is too quiet to really deal with cars, so an external horn of some type might be needed if traffic is a concern. The weight of the bicycle isn't too bad, and the handlebar is pretty short, which is good for storage. The front mudguard is sketchy, so I removed that before I ended up like the other reviewer who got one that wouldn't stay secure. The color mine arrived is is still an ugly matte black, so if you order, don't expect the exact color you see to arrive. Over all, it's a good bike, but TDL will lie to make that sale. Go with somebody else if you can help it.

Afterthought- The matte black paint looks godawful.

Review:
There's so many good things about this bike but let me give you a major reminder that will address many of the negative reviews about this bike:

You need to have some mechanical knowledge of bikes in order to have ANY bike work well. If you don't know how to adjust a rear derailleur or rim brakes, then just be prepared to be frustrated with any bike that has gears or rim brakes...especially at this price.

Ok, with that out of the way, here's the review:

MECHANICAL:
Once you get the rear mech (derailleur) set correctly (meaning the chain is properly in line with the gears) it shifts great and stays in line well. 

The components are great, having a brand like Shimano is always a plus and great to see at this price

The twist shifter is a little firm, my 4 1/2 year old struggled at first to shift, but got the hang of it pretty quick and now has no problem shifting up and down.

The chain stays on well

SIZE:
The size is great, I think it does run a little small for a 20", but in our case that was a good thing because we wanted a bike for him to grow into.

ASSEMBLY:
Assembly was super easy. Ideally I wanted disc brakes to avoid the annoyance of having to regularly adjust the rim brakes, but it is what it is. Can't fault it too much considering the price.

UNIQUE FEATURE:
One of the BEST things about the bike, and honestly it has more to do with me being a mountain biker than my kid actually caring, is the cockpit setup. It has modern style handlebar and stem components just like what you would find on a modern mountain bike. This actually plays a big part in the control that the rider has. Classic/old bikes have the "Y" style handlebars that put the kids hands way above the frame of the bike. All this means is less control, but it's cheaper because they don't have to separately spec out a handlebar/stem that will fit a modern head tube. It might be a small feature, but it sets this bike apart.

OVERALL:
A solid, well performing bike that looks great: all at a great price.

MOST IMPORTANT:
My son loves it, and that's the main thing, right?

Review:
I am a disabled average-height woman and I was able to go on errands with significantly less pain by riding this bike. I had a lot of difficulty setting up this bike because of pain and because the instructions don't include details that I required since I have little technical ability and had never ridden an electric bike or motorcycle. It is important to extend the bike first then raise the seat. I raised the seat first and the bike got jammed when I tried to extend it, so I had to take it to a bike shop to set it up correctly.

The box arrives with tools, so it's not necessary to own tools to do the setup. Yet, I was unable to setup the front wheel correctly. It was not attached to the handlebars. The repairman had to fix that problem also.

I'm glad I got the bike, but I want to warn buyers that the setup procedure is not simple. The bike has a device that has a white light and horn, but I was unable to set it up by myself so I connected it with a spare wire from the packaging. It is not secure and moves forward. Also, when I rode the bike to the supermarket two miles away I realized that I need mirrors, so if you buy this bike you must purchase at least 2 mirrors for safety.

I watched a lot of videos to learn how to setup and ride this bike. To go forward you have to rotate the right handle backwards. To stop or slow the bike you have to rotate the handle forwards. Maybe this is the standard procedure for every scooter, but I had to carefully watch a video several times to figure that out because I have never ridden a motorized vehicle before except the supermarket scooters which have different handlebars.

I strongly recommend practicing on a large flat area such as an empty parking lot to learn how to ride this bike if you are inexperienced. There will be trouble if you are riding on a slanted sidewalk or road, encounter potholes, or there are rocks and other objects on the road. You must be on the alert every second looking at the road surface and watching for cars, people, and animals who might suddenly appear. Also, the ad said this bike goes 15 miles-per-hour but the instruction book said the maximum speed is 13 miles-per-hour.

Review:
I'm a casual bicyclist, and it suits my purposes perfectly. I was going to pay a local bicycle shop to put it together, but they said that it would take a month for them to get to it, so I put it together myself. Turns out assembly was a breeze. The handle bar came pre-assembled with shifters and breaks already attached, I just had to bolt it down. I just needed to add the tires which are quick release and the seat, and it was ready to go! (A mountain bike that I used to own was a nightmare, the gears chattered, the brakes were difficult to adjust and the handle bar was almost impossible to tighten completely, it took forever to assemble, which is why I was willing to pay for the assembly of this one.)
The bike seat wasn’t comfortable at first because I haven’t ridden in years. I just needed to get used to it. It’s fine now.
The shifting is excellent, no chatter. The click shifters are so easy that I don't even think about changing gears when the peddling gets easier or harder. I never had click shifters before, and I don't want to go without them ever again on a bicycle. The grip shifters on my old mountain bike would cause me to accidentally shift gears when I was going over bumps from time to time.
The mountain bikes that I used to own, always felt small like I was trying to ride a child size bike. This hybrid feels like an adult bike to me, and really is a complete joy to ride. I quit riding my last bike when I hit a rock and was thrown over the handle bars and landed on my face. This bike feels like that is less likely to happen. The disc brakes are great, they work when the tires get wet, no slipping!
Even though the hybrid bike is taller than my last mountain bike, it feels lighter. The peddle crank also feels like it's longer than the old mountain bike, giving me a more comfortable stroke, which I like.
For its price, $350, I don't know if I could have gotten a better bike.

Review:
I purchased this bike a year ago.

My advice is have a bike shop tune the bike up immediately when you get it. I got a $35 Groupon bike shop tuneup special, and the bike has not required any further adjustment -- shifts are positive and sure.

Once the bike did try to fold up on me when I was riding it -- I think the fold lock mechanism could be designed better; it has a plastic part that is supposed to lock the mechanism in place. I was not hurt and the bike was not damaged -- I apparently did not quite completely lock it -- but it was a weird experience, like, what is happening here! If you take care to completely lock it, you shouldn't have a problem. For positive locking, I also put a velcro strap around the lock mechanism to hold the lock arm in place, just to be sure.

I kept this bike in my office -- it will fit underneath a table -- and rode it for exercise at lunchtime on occasion. The Schwalbe "Big Apple" tires quite often need more air, so get a hand air pump. The tires are great for urban riding situations (potholes, uneven pavement, etc.).

I had the optional Dahon fenders, front and rear, installed professionally (I probably could have installed them, but just don't have the time). They work well. Nice to know that fenders from Dahon are available should you later decide you need them. Another rear fender option are very cheap rear fenders that clamp to the post. On a folding bike the finders get hit and pushed a lot, so keep that in mind.

I commute by commute train (BART), and this bike can be taken aboard BART trains anytime, even during commute hours.

I have absolutely no regrets with this purchase.

Review:
We got two of those bikes (red and silver) after reading all the positive reviews. Buying experience from 2KSIVER was good though there was several days delay - looked like they were out of stock (though the web site listed them in stock with 5 left). But they answered all emails promptly and did their best to get bikes delivered in time for our vacation.
The bikes came securely packed and almost fully assembled, the red one had a small frame damage but that was not critical. No tools needed - unfold the frame and pedals, turn the seat, install the handlebar, inflate tires and you are ready to go. They do the trick - both easily fit in the back of our Subaru Outback with rear seatbacks down and that was what we needed the folding bikes for. First impression was good, bikes seem well build and ride is relatively comfortable thanks to double suspension. Few negative comments after the first ride:
- Rear derailer in one bike needed adjustment, had to un-tight the cable screw and readjust cable length otherwise the gear number on the hand bar did not correspond with the number of the sprocket.
- In both bikes real derailer guards were bent and prevented switching to gears 5 and 6. Had to manually straighten them. That and the previous problem with derailer would be impossible task for a lot of people with no mechanical skills - means visit to a repair shop.
- Front derailer does not have gear number indication.
- Despite of the alloy frame and rims they are relatively heavy - 34 lb.
- They do not support riders heavier than 200 lb - come on, who they are for, just teens and girls?? should be good for 250 lb at least.
- Both I and my wife found the narrow seats very uncomfortable. Ended up with spending $60 more for two wide soft seats (and Columba does make the wider seats part # 20A for the same price as the original part # 26A ones!). Besides, being 6'2" I had to order a longer 12" seat post separately. It should be possible to select seat post length and seat style while ordering the bikes!
Other than that - nice bikes for the money, overall quality and durability seem to be good.

Review:
This is my first E-Bike, but I have owned many bikes in my life so I can speak to that and the new experience of the electric motor.

At first I did not know what to expect but before I get into my experience, let me highlight my like and dislikes.

+ Design (looks like a motorcycle)
+ Powerful Motor
+ Good Range on 100% motor assist.
+ Integrated LED headlight, taillight, and turn signals.
+ SUPER EASY ASSEMBLY. (Took 5 Min)
+ Twist throttle (better than thumb lever IMO)
+ 28MPH top speed
+ Carries well uphill
+ Saddle leather and color
+ Bike color and finish
- Seat is not comfortable on long rides. (Anything more that 40min)
- No saddle bag or storage (unless you upgrade to the R750)
- No mirrors (must have when commuting on busy streets)
- Small rear taillight/turn signal

This little bicycle is good for leisurely cruises, short commutes, or to ride around the RV / Campsite. I got it to get back into riding bikes to help increase strength in my legs since I have joint problems so long walks are not an option. So this helps me get around and ride longer than I would normally with the electric motor assist modes. The assist has 5 levels, however once you go over 13-15mph, peddling is useless so at that point your just along for the ride.

This bike has good torque, I weigh 225lbs and it pulls me along just fine, the big fat tires does help give the ride more cushion for comfort and load. The seating position is comfortable as long at it is not for too long, but it is tolerable.

COMMUTING:
I used this bike for a few weeks to commute to work. I work about 10 miles from work. On the way to work it half flat with the other half being small to very steep uphill grades. On the return trip the up hills are down hills.
NOTHING BUT MOTOR!! So I wanted to test out the range to work and back, I was able to ride 5 miles around my neighborhood, then ride 11miles to work and back for a total of 27miles and still have 2 bars left on the battery. It took me 34min to get to work (up hills) and 15min to get home (down hills). The commute is mostly long straight roads with some parts being curvy so going full speed was not a problem.

AROUND TOWN:
If you are using this in your local park or streets with other bicyclist and pedestrians learn this bicycle before you get out there. It has fat tires and the turning radius does not make it nimble and if you don't know how to control the throttle or have the proper setting (such as cruise control) things can get dangerous quickly. It is basically an electric motorcycle and can get to 28mph really quickly so it is not a beginners bike for sure.

CLASS 3: E-Bike. (Check your local laws)

GET SAFETY GEAR:

I got myself a great E-bike helmet and some gloves incase I had a mishap. I recommend a good helmet, even a entry level motorcycle helmet is a good option, going 28 mph and being able to reach speeds of up to 40mph down hill, I would protect my head and wear some good jeans and a jacket. I ride at night too so I added flashing rear light to increase visibility.

All in all it is a great little E-bike, the convenience of 5 min assembly out the box and the on demand power with most of the bells and whistle make this a good option for a bike rider that is getting into the electric vehicle world.

Hope this was helpful!

I bought this bike in both black and white (my boyfriend and I wanted matching bikes) to ride around town. I live in Idaho where there are several inclines so i wanted something with multiple speeds. I'll admit i was wary about ordering an item that had less than 4 stars. (When looking for items on Amazon, I generally go to filters and hit both prime eligible and 4 stars+ to weed out any iffy items.) I

am so glad that I purchased this item! I haven't found any problems with either bike so far. When we received the bikes, they were in slightly varied states of assembly. After a few minutes of putting the bikes together, we realized that, although we knew what we were doing, the bikes would need to be tuned up by someone who REALLY knew what they were doing. BRING YOUR BIKE TO A PROFESSIONAL. They found all sorts of little things that we would not have noticed. Since these bikes are cheaper, they obviously aren't guaranteed great assembly in the warehouse. The only one truly negative thing the bike shop had to say was that the gear shifter was cheaply made so shifting could be a problem but that it wasn't a safely hazard.

Since we have been riding, my boyfriend and I haven't had a single problem! We ride a minimum of a mile each time we ride and both get to our destination safely and in a great mood! People in the previous reviews have complained that the brakes are poor, that they don't coast for very long, etc., but we haven't had a single problem and I'm crediting that to the fact that we had ours professionally worked on. We were a little concerned how hard it might be to ride a bike with such small wheels (smaller wheel base=a lot more peddling) but we wanted the bikes for more exercise and although we have to pedal more than a bike with 26" wheels, we don't find that we are much more tired on these bikes than normal! We love them!

This bike has been a hit to everyone who has never seen a folding bike before. I love folding it up for those who are curious and it is SO SIMPLE to do! it takes me a little longer than a minute but that's because I'm weak handed and very cautious. haha Otherwise neither my boyfriend or I have trouble folding or unfolding the bikes. I did have a problem with my seat not wanting to stay up but with a little tweaking, I no longer have that problem! (I'm 5'6" and weigh 170 lb). When folded up, both our bikes fit in the back seat of his standard sized car no problem!

The bike weighs around 30 to 35 pounds which to some may seem like a lot but both my boyfriend and I carry our bikes up the flight of stairs to our apartment relatively easily. Once again, it's a good workout!

As for the bike seat, yes, your butt will hurt at first. Mine did the first few rides! But right about the time I decided I was going to buy a different seat, i found that my butt didn't hurt nearly as much and now it's actually relatively comfortable. Give it a chance; break in the seat! (Ice your butt if you have to the first few times. haha)

My only complaint are 1: the gear shifter - I am a bit weary about changing gears much because it feels a little sensitive. Mind you, it hasn't given me any problems. 2: The smaller wheel base takes some getting used to, but I expected that. Since the tires are much smaller than traditional adult bikes, the turn radius is much smaller so it's easy to over-turn and throw yourself out of balance. Make sure to practice a bit before going out there and racing someone around the neighborhood.

This bike has tried to kill me on a regular basis. It started off ok, and then after about half a year, the bottom bracket gave out. This means that now, when I put too much force into pedaling (usually at high speeds) the pedals will "skip", causing my feet to slip off, resulting in... pain.

Handlebar screws: Remember how I said the bottom bracket broke, well when it does throw me off, the handle bars rotate in their attachment, because the screws loosen themselves, and without a something to brace myself on, I get thrown over the handlebars.

Also, if you get this bike, be sure to swap out the brake pads. Something about them will make it so they are unable to grip the rim of your tire well.

Finally, the derailleur are absolute crap. the front one doesnt have the range to effectively reach all 3 gears, so I have had to adjust it to just work on the first 2, and the back one only works for the middle range of gears.Because the bottom bracket is broken my bike pedals wobble when i pedal, and this wobble can shift the front gears for me in between strokes, which causes more skipping.

Well, that covers just about every component on the bike that I've had trouble with, and just about every component on the bike as well.

The bike looks like a regular bike and rides like one too. No need to turn the battery on if you would like to get some exercise and ride around the town. Review:
UPDATE: Two years later and I still love it!!

This bike has lots of advantages: It is manageable (I'm 68 and can lift it with some effort), it is a blast to ride on electric, and it's pretty stable and comfortable. I'm definitely glad I bought it, as it gets me outside and gives me exercise I enjoy. But it is not perfect. For one, I had to take it to a bike shop because the brake pads and brake plates didn't line up. No matter how I fiddled with it, the brakes were always applied which made peddling hard. I wish I could say they fixed it, but they were only able to make it better, so peddling is still kind of hard, no matter which gear I am in. The other thing is the peddle-assist. The truth is that no matter how soft or slow you peddle, even on the lowest setting the assist mode will take over and will take you faster than you can peddle. That's fine if you want to go fast, but if you're looking for exercise, you can't use the peddle assist at all. So when I switch it on, I take it off peddle assist mode which allows me to use the grip as a throttle (like on a motorcycle), and I alternate between unassisted peddling, or going without peddling and only using the throttle. I find the latter very useful for taking off from a complete stop, as well as switching into when I am on a rough road or when I start to tire. So I've found a way to make it work for me. But it would have been nice to be able to use the peddle assist mode. The other thing is the adjustables, especially the seat and handlebar height. I find that if I have the adjustment levers loose enough that I can close them, the seat or handlebar just slides down to the lowest level. But if I tighten the lever, I can't close it. So I find I have to stop several times in a trip to readjust the height of either the seat or the handlebar.

I made some adjustments. I found the grip on the peddles too aggressive, so I switched them out for peddles with a less aggressive grip that also fold, which makes it more convenient to store in the car trunk. I cut off the rubber end of one of the handles and inserted a rear view mirror, which, frankly, I don't see how I can live without. I added a softer seat which really helps.

The inconveniences I mentioned are not deal-killers. They are annoyances or disappointments. I still love the bike and would recommend it to anyone who is looking for a fun ride, for exercise, for beating city traffic and avoiding public transportation during Covid. I love that I can peddle as far as I want and still be certain to make it home because I can ride myself back on electric. This freedom is fantastic.

I don't think either brakes or gear shifter are well suited for young riders. Our six your old struggles to have enough strength to change gears. In fact I've only seen her succeed in shifting gears once or twice. The brakes are another big problem. The levers extend way too far away from the handle bar. For me, this is a huge problem because it's safety related. She has to take her hand off the handle bar in order to grab the brake. I've tried adjusting the brakes so the levers are closer to the handle bar, but they are still far from ideal.

Finally, assembly of the bike was pretty easy but I still had to spend two nights doing it. This is because the wheels were horribly out of true. I had to make large adjustments to the spokes in order to true the wheels. It was also kind of tedious because I don't have a trueing stand.

My recommendation is to avoid this bike unless you have kids with large strong hands and you have a bunch of time to tinker.

Review:
Just received the Giordano Libero 1.6 - 56cm today (it's for my daughter, she's 5'9") and I must admit I am impressed, and my daughter absolutely LOVES IT! The pictures do not do justice to this bike, it truly is a nice piece of equipment.

Some of the details that are not easily seen in the pictures are, for example, the handlebar tape, it looks like typical white tape but it's a nice soft and textured tape with a tropical (floral) pattern on it, as it gets dirty the pattern slowly appears. The "o's" of the name (Giordano) have the Italian flag colors in them. Between the red and white parts of the bike there's a section in black with the word "libero" repeated several times in a discreet and elegant pattern. The Velo seat is actually fairly comfortable, and has a very nice race design to it, including a measurement scale on the rails to fine tune your seat placement (forward or backwards). The crankarms are white as well (really nice touch!).

In all aspects this bike looks and feels like a much more expensive bike than it is. The integrated shifters/brakes (or brifters) are quite nice and work exceptionally well after being properly adjusted and the shift indicators are easy tho see since they are bright pink/red on the black background. The Shimano 2300 front and rear derailleurs are good entry level quality (lowest level for Shimano, but still good overall) for anyone trying out road cycling and the wheels, albeit heavy, are strong enough for the typical beginner rider to work with. The 6061 aluminum frame is strong and yielding enough for recreational purposes (I believe it's the same frame as the GMC Denali Pro, same angles and material but the Libero is MUCH MUCH nicer in appearance due to the Italian inspired racing designs - both bikes are made by Kent Cycles).

Assembly was quite easy for anyone with some experience with bikes but if you want this bike to perform at its best (and you're not familiar with fine tuning) you should take it to your local bike shop to get it running perfectly. I was amazed that the wheels were true right out of the box (but surprised that they were Schrader valves instead of Presta) Also, this is the type of bike that if you start getting serious about putting lots of miles on it you can slowly upgrade components with the help and advice of any decent bike shop out there.

Now, there's three items that are somewhat disappointing about this bike, but they're not that big of a deal. First, the pedals, they are heavy and the typical steel "shin scrappers", with no toe clips or straps, which was weird because the GMC Denali Pro (which is in all ways is a cheaper bike) has decent clip/strap pedals included (entry level stuff). The second thing are the brakes, they work fine but they are "ugly" and clunky and don't have a quick release system on them, it's something odd since everything else on this bike is quite nice and clean, another oddity about the Libero is that the GMC Denali Pro has actually "nice" Tektro brakes (entry level stuff) with quick releases... If Kent only had put the pedals and brakes of the Denali Pro on the Libero 1.6 this Giordano bike would've been as close to a perfect buy/value/performance as you could get. Lastly, the fork, even though it's an all aluminum frame, the fork is made out of steel, it's strong but heavier, unfortunately this is a little costlier to upgrade, but all in all it functions as it should.

So, if you want to do some immediate, and somewhat inexpensive upgrades, to make this bike feel and ride like an excellent road bike I would recommend upgrading the brakes (something less clunky and lighter) and pedals to toe clips/straps or even better go with clipless (this will cost a little more due to the purchase of the pedals and specific shoes) also take off the kickstand to shave a little weight off too and of course, talk to your local shop.

The Giordano Libero 1.6 will not disappoint the entry level road cyclist.

This bike earned five stars from our household because it's a good-looking, thoughtfully designed option for small kids who want a big-kid ride. Here's what we liked about it:

-- This bike looks more like a mountain bike. There are no plastic shields with cartoon characters and no silly padded bars.

With this bike, he was riding without trainers within minutes.
-- Our son loves the bell, and we like the handle on the back of the seat. It makes the bike easier to load into the truck for family bike rides.

We had one complaint: one of the pedals cracked after a few weeks. They were of a standard size, so we substituted one from an old bike. Overall, build quality on this bike is good.

So, if you're looking for a nice-looking "big kid" bike for your little rider, the Royalbaby is a fine choice.

Review:
We ordered this balance bike for our 18 month old daughter who outgrew her smaller balance bike. This bike is a good fit for her. The bike stands at 17" from ground to handlebars and 11" from ground to seat. The wheels are made of plastic. The back wheels are 5 3/4" in diameter and 1 1/2" wide. The front wheel is 8"inches in diameter and 2" wide. The rear wheels are spaced about 3" apart to try and provide some stability while your child rides the balance bike.

What we like:

- The height is perfect for our short 18 month old daughter. The handlebars are also at the the perfect height.

- The wheels roll quite smoothly and do not need air.

- The handlebars are limited as to how far they turn to prevent the bike from tipping over.

- Assembly was easy.

What we don't like:

- We were disappointed with several things about this bike. The first disappointment is that we did not receive the color that we ordered. We ordered a pink balance bike, but received a green bike instead.

- The tires or made of solid plastic. When your child tries to mount on a hard surface, the bike likes to kick out from under them because the tires do not grip. This also happens when they dismount the bike and occasionally when they turn. At the very least, these tires need a rubber band around the wheels so they grip the hard surface when mounting or dismounting the bike.

- The bike is made of cheap plastic. The seat and fenders bend easily. The front fender started showing stress marks (see picture) from the children pushing on the front fender.

- The wheels have a vent hole which allows water to collect inside if it sits in a puddle. The water does drain, but if it sits too long without drying out, it could begin to cause mold problems inside the wheel.

This could be a very good balance bike if the manufacturer wouldn't cut corners on the quality of materials used to make the bike. This bike tips way too easily because of the cheap, hard plastic tires that have no grip. With the issue of the hard plastic tires and the cheap plastic seat and fender, it was all we could do to find enough reasons to give this bike a 3-star rating.

Review:
This bike is BEAUTIFUL!!! Just got it today and took it for a quick spin around the neighborhood with my wife, this was the birthday gift I got her. I'll jump right in and give you my first impressions.

PROS:
- Its extremely sturdy and well built. I'm actually shocked at the quality of the frame and the components. Thick down tubes and good welds everywhere, I think I'm going to get years of use from this bad boy.
- It comes nearly fully assembled. Start to finish, it took me less than an hour to put it together. They've done most of the tricky stuff and you really just have to situate the front tire, the seats and the handle bars.
- Super wide tires. I plan on keeping this at our shore house because it doesn't have gears and flat ground is where this thing needs to be. The wide, white wall tires are gonna be perfect for the occasional patch of sand and I shouldn't get bogged down, that's just a bad accident waiting to happen with two people on a bike when you lose control of the front tire. These fatties should cruise right over.
- The paint is perfect. No low spots or missed coverage. In fact, even the handle bars, seat posts and all other metal pieces I can see have been coated, there's no bare metal anywhere. This should keep visible rust at bay and keep the entire bike looking sharp for a long time.
- I'm a big guy, 6'3, 200 pounds, and I'm very comfortable on this bike. I was able to raise the seat pretty high and the handle bars come back to you pretty far so you'll be seated completely upright and look like royalty as you glide down the road.
- The kickstand. Trust me, it's perfect.

CONS:
- No tools included. You don't need a lot, but if you don't have Allen wrenches in your aresenal, you're going to need to get your hands on some (add them to your order, they don't take up a lot of space in a junk drawer and you'll be surprised how much you use them for other things). You're also going to need a few, different sized wrenches. I think the manufacturer should have included these specific items in the set, but I'm guessing their exclusion lends to the lower price of the bike.
- The pedals. They're great looking out of the box, but aside from the post being metal, the pedal itself is plactic. I forsee this plastic getting brittle over time and snapping off. I'll eventually upgrade mine anyways. If you swap yours out, be mindful that the width of the screw is SMALLER on the rear crankset. If you put this bike together, you'll know what I mean.

That's it, the pros far outweigh the cons.

Review:
I waited a bit to provide my review of two Eahora bicycles. I wanted a 100+ miles of use before evaluating my first e-bike. Prior to these bikes both my wife and I road Specialized hardtail mountain bikes for years.
We purchased the EX100 (26 inch tires) and the AM 100 (27.5 tires) In general we could not be more happy regarding the bikes. I am pretty old, so I do not do off road mountain biking any longer. My wife never did. The bikes are capable of trail riding, but I would get the EX 100 should that be your activity choice. The AM 100 while a more sophisticated bike is a bit more difficult to handle on trails due to its size and my age (70+ - I have no business on mountain trails any longer). The EX 100 is far more nimble and responsive, though both are capable bikes.
I can not over praise the 48v, 10.4 amp battery. We have charged them once in our 100+ miles. We use them strictly to assist on hill climbing. They do hold a charge. I can crank it up to over 20+ mph with battery assist on level ground and the 350 watt motor will provide a lot of help on steeper hills (We live in the Ozarks of Northwest Arkansas). In all fairness, the 500 watt motor was not available when we purchased the bikes or I would have gone for it on the AM 100.
The bikes we easy to assemble, but the written instructions were pretty skimpy. I used U-Tube tutorials when necessary. The bikes were well packaged, save the battery, which was floating free in the box on both bikes. One of the battery end caps was cracked. Eahors’s customer service was responsive and persistent, even though I ended up effecting the repair by my choice. I am satisfied with the outcome.
The bottom line is I would purchase a bike from this company again without reservation. They make a quality product at a reasonable price. They have solid customer service. I trust the bikes will last many years.
